items.body: The Romanian collective Nam-Khar has been active since 2009, releasing numerous albums and collaborations over the years. In recent years, much of their work has appeared on labels such as Zazen Sounds, Winter-Light, and, more recently, Cyclic Law. With this new release, Nam-Khar explores a concept centered on alchemy, specifically the transformation of the self; the connection to—and inspiration drawn from—psychoanalytic pioneers such as Freud and Jung is therefore evident. It is no coincidence that the album comprises seven tracks, a number of symbolic significance in alchemy. Here, Nam-Khar gives free rein to their creativity. While the music remains rooted in the Ritual genre, it is clearly much more than that. It incorporates strong Dark-Ambient elements alongside Industrial sounds and a pronounced Cinematic influence, manifesting itself primarily in deep, astral passages. Add a healthy dose of experimentation to the mix, and you get a sense of the highly diverse “Antimon”, where magical analogue sounds, acoustic instruments, and field recordings converge. The album oscillates between mysterious, dreamlike passages and others that are menacing and ominous. With “Antimon”, Nam-Khar once again delivers a compelling release that is sure to captivate a wider audience interested in the aforementioned genres. (Rating:8). Listen to “Melanosis”: Melanosis by Nam-Khar About Nam-Khar Nam-Khar is a ritual ambient project centered on Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009. The project debuted with “A Hallowed Ground Within” the same year, and its catalog mixes ritual and dark ambient with industrial and cinematic elements, built from ethnic instrumentation, analog synthesis and field recordings. Nam-Khar released “Secret Essence / Sangwa Dupa” (CD, Winter-Light) in 2018 and “Sur Chöd” (Winter-Light) in 2020, followed by “Dok-Pa” (Zazen Sounds) in 2022, a sequence Cyclic Law describes as the project’s “Tibetan Trilogy”. The same year brought “Nag-Hammadi” (Winter-Light), a collaboration with Vortex. Nam-Khar has also recorded with Alone in the Hollow Garden and Sielwolf, releasing “The Sarajevo Spiral” with Vortex and “Antariksha” as Alone In The Hollow Garden & Nam-Khar, both in 2024. With “Antimon”, released July 20, 2026 on Zazen Sounds and Cyclic Law, Nam-Khar returns after “The Sarajevo Spiral” with a seven-track album built around an alchemical concept.

items.body: There’s nothing so startling as the appearance of a vintage concert tape, in this case some 47 years old, that might illumine your view of a musician’s oeuvre, even a slight shift in focus counting for much. Such is the case with the release of Cecil Taylor’s performance from a New Mexico concert in 1979. Part of the concert was lost, but on the evidence heard here, Taylor was at the helm of one of the finest groups he would ever lead, a relatively unusual quintet that consisted of alto saxophonist Jimmy Lyons (with Andrew Cyrille, one of Taylor’s greatest collaborators), drummer Jerome Cooper and two string players, the violinist Ramsay Ameen and Alan Silva, here playing cello as well as his usual bass. Among extant releases, the two-LP set bears some resemblance, at least in personnel, to It Is in the Brewing Luminous , recorded in 1980 at New York’s Fat Tuesday’s, which had the additional inclusion of drummer Sunny Murray in the band and Alan Silva playing bass, exclusively. His cello playing here is an essential element, especially for the way in which it combines with Ameen’s violin. In a sense, the Albuquerque quintet is a larger band than the New York sextet, in terms of what the opening up of the soundscape makes possible. Perhaps the most notable thing about the Albuquerque recording is the level of subtle and evolving detail achieved by the quintet and its capture in the extraordinary recording job done by Mike Wolff, who was regularly responsible for recording the New Mexico Symphony Orchestra. The University of New Mexico’s Steinway was also borrowed for the performance, giving Taylor a piano appropriate to his special energies. The unusual clarity with which Ameen is heard here gives the performance some of its special significance, particularly in the way that his contribution combines with Silva’s cello in a virtual string section. Jerome Cooper, too, is less polyrhythmic, less aggressive than his predecessor, Andrew Cyrille, who had been the perfect complement in the trio with Taylor and Lyons. What is highlighted here is the omni-directionality of Taylor’s music, from his thorough absorption of Western “classical” music as well as the jazz tradition and the general legacy of African music in America. Here those elements are present both individually and in Taylor’s special syntheses, those combined and foregrounded strings every bit as African as they are European. Side C is given over to one of Taylor’s trance rituals, a summoning of spirits -- equivalent perhaps to speaking in tongues -- inspired and unknowable language accompanied by incidental phrases from the instruments, random sounds and Taylor’s piano musings, now enacted directly on the instrument’s strings, all an essential component of the complexity and mystery of Taylor’s far-reaching art. The music that continues on side D is particularly spacious, opening up with Cooper’s spare percussion and the lyrical motifs of Ameen, Lyons and Taylor, evolving and flowering, still spacious yet dense with high speed content – some of Taylor’s most brilliant moments on record, the other instruments lifted skyward, until it concludes with Taylor’s gravelly equivalent of speaking in tongues, the very practice akin to the untranslatability of Taylor’s complex, contrapuntal, poly-vocal band music and the extrapolating lines and abstract organizing figures with which he guides the music from his piano keyboard. Live at the KiMo Theater is a special event, reasserting an especially creative and relatively neglected period in Taylor’s career. Live at the KiMo Theater will be released on October 16th, but you can listen to a track and pre-order now . Live at the KiMo Theater Albuquerque 1979 by Cecil Taylor Unit Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items.body: ‘Speechless’ is Resina’s first standalone album in three years. On her latest record, Warsaw-based cellist and composer Karolina Rec massively expands on her sound, which includes ideas of language, the role of the voice, and the ever-changing aspects of nature. The nine pieces are entangled with cello, voice, and electronics. Drummer Mateusz Rychlicki joins in with the 23-piece 441 Hz Choir, while Magdalena Gajdzica plays flute and Micha? Fojcik includes field recordings and additional sound design. Speechless is actually quite the opposite of its title, as the record is all about finding one’s voice. Resina has without doubt found hers. Her voice emerges from darkly-lit alleyways and the snake-charming essence of the flute seems to evoke mysteries beyond mortal comprehension. Pulsating electronics and insidious undercurrents are present throughout the running time, with the voice elongating and sometimes even shrieking, as if it were a victim of age-old torture methods. Its austere beauty is speckled with sudden shifts in mood and drops in temperature. The unpredictability of nature – of everything, in fact – is in evidence when the tones suddenly sink and transform, plagued by a sudden scratching rhythm and the nitro-fuelled drumming. Sirens enter and create mass anxiety, adding to feelings of imminent destruction. This also accelerates the intensity of the music, and at times it can be an absolute monster. Speechless is a dark album, and it purposely throws into doubt the direction of its music: is it lost for words, or are the words trapped, in agony, and unable to be voiced? Is there some kind of asphyxiation taking place within its echoing wails and howls? Speechless, it seems, is a record in some distress. The choir brings a reverence to its music, sometimes standing alone and being surrounded by a glimmering halo of prime light. But even here, distortions and subtle pitch-shifts exist, ready to invade at any second. The pitch drops like a bomb, collapsing again and again. Resina finds her voice in the music’s flair for intensity and powerful movement; perhaps the music can speak after all, and what it has to say is so powerful that it takes the breath away. Speechless releases on FatCat’s 130701 imprint on November 19. www.resina.bandcamp.com

items.body: William Fowler Collins invites you into his Field Music (SIGE, October 19), a dark and minimal dream sequence from New Mexico, where slow, mystical drones are embedded into the fabric of rhythmic diversity, pulled together by dark, mysterious intentions. Inseparable from the album is the history of the atomic bomb, as evidenced from the photograph on the cover, which shows the ranch where the first nuclear weapon was assembled. Field Music relates to the patter of the military drum corps, an incessant battle cry of a tribe in motion, and a sound which hovers over a rainy and sustained drone that blends into the polyrhythms of Voodoo ritual. Collins notes that the titular field can also be defined as the fabric of time and space. A contradiction runs through the sound, as although the music is minimal, the space the drone creates is epic and desert-like, mirroring the geography of New Mexico; a sound which is both restrictive and largely concealed, but wide enough to dilate the pupils. Convulsing with regular upheavals, the rhythms become a slowly developing form of hypnotism. Field Music pulls you in with its unstoppable gravity. Once inside, it’s impossible to get out, to remove oneself, like prey caught up in a spider’s silver web. Looping out of the machine, these sustained drones quiver in their subtle oscillations and their repetitive regurgitations. Pushing itself outwards, the drone continues to loop on with a steely stare, an unforgiving glare of a cruel deity. The title track’s rhythms have an urgency to them, but the steady pulses of ‘Contact Is A Mother’ slow things down, revolving, whirring, like the blades of a military chopper seconds away from its doom. Rhythm is primal, inbuilt, prehistoric. Its connection to the body is as deep and as essential as its relationship with the internal organs; its raw, carnivorous energy is released in the form of dance or uncontrolled physical movement, which is a response to its possession, and the only appropriate one to an invading presence. The regular strobes are felt more than heard, and that’s especially true of ‘How Horrible It Would Be’, where the drone lurks in a dark and deep tunnel, using the lower bass frequencies as a lair. The rhythm churns in the distance, but it feels so alive, reeking of ancient history and the ever-shifting revolutions of the present. ‘They Wept Together’ has more of a 4/4 pattern, but even this is dissected by a quicker rhythm that nestles deep within the track, rhythm inside rhythm inside rhythm inside rhythm; a musical house of leaves. www.williamfowlercollins.com

items.body: Hekla’s haunting theremin evokes the cold and magical depths of Iceland. On Á, the Icelander uses her theremin in such a way as to conjure up a plethora of ancient spirits under a neon-green swirl of northern lights. Hekla Magnúsdóttir is a devoted pupil of the instrument; this makes her more than adept, putting her into the range of a master. She’s an expert when it comes to playing and manipulating its air. Her dedication and study has given rise to enviable, supreme levels of skill, and while it’s hard not to be affected by the ghostly, spectral qualities of the instrument, it’s capable of being so much more than that. It’s capable of great emotion and intelligence, not just to accompany an episode of Most Haunted or a trashy Halloween weekender on TV; what the stereotypes of popular culture would have you believe. Hekla shows the listener the emotional capabilities of the instrument with equal elevations of intensity and finesse. In saying that, there’s something incredibly eerie and fragile in its sound. There’s no denial. Bold and distinctive, Hekla’s haunting music has that wow factor, which is all the more impressive on a debut, but it also develops an experimental side with its clashing tones and intermittent noise-clusters, only to slip into a spacious and peaceful zone where the theremin ghostly levitates, clothed in nothing but the night. Her voice rises and falls, in tune and in time with the spooky (and queasy) dips. The music cries with the repetitious chorus of whale-song. Hekla gently unsettles and stirs up the folklore of the land. It’s an intense ride – and her current Berlin residence gives the music a propulsive, contemporary electronic edge, as dark as many of the music’s German electronic sisters, but at the same time set apart purely because of the theremin’s presence. While there’s plenty of power and roar to its revolutions, it’s also capable of shutting down and giving in – giving up – to sadness. The theremin cries in the black of the dark, a lone shudder of electricity and a desolate lament, a hymn where verses are seared in painful yowls and a mile-wide loneliness. It feels like an outsider – instrumentally, at least – occupying a stretch of deserted road. But its individuality is also a cause for celebration, and a blessing. It moves through life as a solo entity, roaming the wilds of Iceland in search of something that may never be found. Contrasting this is her angelic, ever-echoing voice, which is a source of precious light in the frozen hinterlands of resolute snowfall and bitter ice. She brings the theremin out of its shell, away from its séances and shadows, without dissolving any of its mystery. Á will be released September 14 on Phantom Limb. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Alex Kourelis has been active as Digital Geist since 1999. The American artist has even collaborated with none other than Patrick Codenys of Front 242 on a joint album. Now, after a relatively quiet period, he returns with “Starcrashed”. This is a conceptual work—more specifically, an alternative Soundtrack that Alex K. composed for the 1979 film “Starcrash”. He analyzed the film scene by scene to create his own score, resulting in no fewer than 36 tracks and a total running time of around 90 minutes. From the very first notes, it is clear that this is a Soundtrack. However, anyone expecting conventional film music with orchestral arrangements and sweeping strings is in for a surprise. Digital Geist has always incorporated strong Electro influences, and this release is no exception. There is a generous dose of EBM, alongside Industrial elements, Acid sequences, nods to Techno, and even hints of Psy-Trance. Naturally, most of the tracks are extremely short. While this can sometimes be a little frustrating, it is inevitable given the concept behind the album. It is a shame, though, because the shorter tracks often contain some of the best material, with certain passages evoking the atmosphere of the Chemical Brothers or Praga Khan at their best. I was also particularly impressed by the superb mixing and powerful production, which sound truly ultra-professional. The only downside is that, although there are some longer pieces, I find these to be the least interesting tracks on the album. It is a unique concept—one could easily describe it as an EBM Soundtrack—and the kind of project that makes you wish more films or series would feature this style of music. Last but not least, the limited-edition USB release also includes the original film accompanied by this alternative Soundtrack. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Hard Time In Space”: https://digitalgeist.bandcamp.com/track/hard-time-in-space

items.body: These are liner notes by Stef Gijssels for two recent albums by Swedish saxophonist and composer Martin Küchen, first with Angles 4, second for his solo album. Angles 4 - (Relative Pitch, 2026) Listening to Angles 4 here and now, in 2026, feels like a warm homecoming. The album is filled with the grand themes that have resonated throughout the various ensembles over the years, from the Martin Küchen Trio and Angles 6 to Angles 9 and All Included . The quartet knows this material by heart, having performed these compositions for decades. I would almost call them their personal standards: they sound deeply familiar, yet they retain the same power and vigour as they must have had at their very first performances—perhaps now with even greater maturity, intensity and fierceness. The smaller quartet format gives the musicians more room to explore, express and expand, particularly across the relatively long tracks, most of which run for seven or eight minutes. There is a sense of space in the arrangements, but never a loss of urgency. The music digs deep into the history of jazz, drawing on the spirit of Mingus and Coltrane, while at times reaching even further back into the history of sound itself—and into the collective emotions of people living through dire times: war, oppression and other horrors. Here, music becomes both a source of comfort and a force of liberation. Whatever the size of the ensemble, this music remains as infectious as ever. Listen and download from Bandcamp Martin Küchen - Chase The Demons Out (Thanatosis, 2026) Brutal sounds. Heart-rending, bleak. Gut-wrenching and abrasive. Sorrowful, dark, mournful, ominous. One musician generating a torrent of expression through three instruments played at once: sopranino saxophone, two horizontal hand drums, along with cymbals, metal plates, and bowls. We know Martin Küchen from his work with the Angles ensemble—music that unfolds in epic arcs, sweeping themes that speak to a collective emotional space. This is the opposite. Here the music is stripped down to brutal poetry: visceral, concise, unadorned. Short, explosive statements. Limited means used to build intense dramatic pressure. Küchen’s anger at the state of the world is well known, and here it finds direct form in pounding drums and the wailing saxophone. Sound bursts collide and fracture, channeling raw fury. The opening track, “ Chase The Demons Out, ” reflects a world drifting toward totalitarianism. Its title echoes a phrase from 1970s Chinese state media calling to “sweep away all demons”—to eliminate those who think differently. The theme feels disturbingly current as war again ravages the Middle East, where rockets, aircraft, and attack drones serve the ambitions of those in power. The second piece, “ Mach kein Krach ” (“stop making noise”), recalls Küchen’s father telling him to quiet down as a child—something his son clearly had no intention of doing. The message is the opposite of silence: make your voice heard. Refuse passivity. Rebel, resist, speak up. Make noise. The third piece, “ Mit Ach und Krach, ” uses a German expression describing something achieved with great difficulty—through blood, sweat, and tears. Speaking out and resisting the present state of affairs demands exactly that kind of effort. Taken together, the three brief pieces form a suite: anger at the world, inner rebellion, and the search for the energy to act. Every saxophone cry, every drum strike carries elemental emotion—horror, pain, rejection, fear—pushed forward by outrage, anger, disgust, and indignation. These forces build toward movement: to resist, to act, to stand together. It will take effort. It will take blood, sweat, and tears. Once again, Küchen shows his artistic clarity. The music is raw, brutal, uncompromising—and authentic. The world needs this." Listen and download from Bandcamp Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: From solo piano to orchestra, the music in this genre bears witness to life’s atrocities; it reflects the change of seasons; it seeks to console and uplift. Our top pick reintroduces us to a fallen friend, but new composers make an impact as well; one can never tell where the next great album will come from. Soon the leaves will begin to fall again, and then the snow, and then the rain, and then it will be summer. These composers bring us through life’s transitions, always looking forward to the next, teaching us the wisdom of cycles through the beauty of notes. Our cover image is taken from Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador, covered below. Jóhann Jóhannsson has been gone nearly a decade now, and his absence is still felt. After a trickle of posthumous releases, we had grown resigned to the thought that we might never again hear new music from the composer. Meanwhile, Adam Wiltzie was working on unfinished pieces from a collaboration begun before the composer’s untimely death. We can think of no one better to tackle such a project. Adding to the sadness is the knowledge that Steve Albini helped with the production before he too was lost to the sands of time. Friendship Survival Guide is a tribute and a sonic keepsake; it’s a minor miracle that it exists at all. The first video is the beginning of a narrative thread; we can’t wait to see the rest! (Deutsche Grammophon, September 18). Also on Deutsche Grammophon, Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir reimagines her back catalogue with Robert Ames and the DSO Berlin. This Will Be Us breathes new life into these pieces and is preceded by non-album track “Floods” (October 23). The cover of Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador looks like Max from Where the Wild Things Are sleeping off his evening; but it may also be a young man dreaming of adventure. The album is an ode to childhood imagination, bolstered by copious choirs and swirling strings (Arts & Crafts, September 25). Third Coast Percussion returns with Vernacular, the percussion ensemble’s 25th album. Jlin is now a full performing member, as heard on the opening single Premonition (Rockwell, October 23). Klara Lewis‘ Opening is already out, one of autumn’s early highlights. The album is awash in shades of blue, from art to music. After the abraded loops of “Ta Min Hand “, the set moves from form to abstraction, shifting like light through falling leaves (Editions Mego, September 4).   Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen is a diverse set that addresses migration and memory through song, spoken word, voice and field recordings. The artist’s cello shines throughout the set, which culminates in a surprising rendition of “Shchedryk,” known to modern listeners as “Carol of the Bells” (Alumni Records Glasgow, September 4). Earlier this year, cellist Gaspar Claus impressed us with the score to French film Un Monde Violent. Now he returns with CELLS, which includes a contribution from Matt Elliott (Third Eye Foundation). The album is released September 25 on InFiné. Inspired by the work of visual artist James Turrell, Alyssa Weinberg‘s Pieces of Light, performed by cellist Gabriel Cabezas, plays with permutations of illumination. The album is preceded by the single ultraviolet (MASS MoCA, October 2).   Clerestory reflects its title, which refers to the windows in the upper section of walls, as found in churches. Jules Reidy uses this image to color the music, which highlights the interplay between shadow and light and whose single-track Side A is brought to light by JACK Quartet (Thrill Jockey, September 25). Twin Cities four-piece The Dust of Suns Ensemble offers Alyosha is a series of miniatures, inspired by Dostoyevsky, but with a playful aura. Released on September 1, early copies of the album are available on precious 10″ vinyl. We don’t receive many hurdy-gurdy albums, much less albums of hurdy-gurdy with violin and cello. Almost Starlight is one of these, recorded in a medieval church by Jem Finer (yes, that Jem Finer, from The Pogues!), John Matthias and Jay Auborn. The results are magical, mystical and ceremonial (Touch, September 4). Simon Goff‘s electronic chamber music is packed with violin and viola, with guest appearances by Anne Müller on cello. Interior Realms – vol. 1 is upbeat and life-affirming, on the surface a study of architecture but beneath this a treatise on the soul (Sonic Pieces, September 10). We can never tell where more eaze will head next, which is part of her appeal. On valley and structure, she heads for the heart of modern composition, even offering a score booklet. A host of guest starts decorates the set with new timbres and additional grace (Thrill Jockey, October 9).   Goldmund‘s In Each Moment is a gorgeous fall collection, inspired by the teachings of Buddhist nun Sister Dang Nghiem. The piano notes are as delicate as incense wafting to the sky, enhanced by some gentle ambient textures, producing a sense of perfect peace (Nettwerk, October 9). Chad Lawson‘s lowercase hush is as serene as can be, a prelude to winter. On held by evening, one can hear the almost hear the leaves as they start to fall (Decca, September 11). Jumping straight into that faraway season, Volodja Brodsky‘s piano-based Winterglare recalls the sun’s low angle in Estonia’s winter (We Are Busy Bodies, October 2). Piano player meets machine on The End is a Beginning, from the aptly named Postmodern Machine. The beats are warm and plentiful, but the ivories still hold court (Moderna, September 11). Some may recall that Björk’s first film role was in the feminist retelling of the Grimm tale The Juniper Tree. Forty years after it was written by Nietzchka Keene, the film receives a new score from Midori Hirano. The artist manages to tap into the tenderness and leans into the unsettling tension, with piano as the anchor and synthesizer as the encroachment (Viernulvier/Thrill Jockey, October 2). Ingfrid Breie Nyhus‘ Silkegul – Slåttepiano III is the third in a series of albums that investigate Norwegian folk traditions by means of the piano. As the nights grow longer, the notes will seem more and more fitting, like tales told around a fire (Lab, October 9).   Billed as a classical soul pianist, Alexis Ffrench releases the lush 24, two dozen pieces meant to comprise the soundtrack of a day. With tracks such as In Flight, crossover success is virtually guaranteed (Sony Classical, October 2). Pianist Sofi Paez releases Bodies of Water, inspired by Iceland’s diversity of natural beauty. Ocean is the first single (OPIA Community, September 25). Doubts and Loves Like a Mole is the new EP from pianist Nathan Schubert, preceded by the peaceful, brass-inflected single Schillerpromenade (Bigo & Twigeitti, October 2). Brandon Hopkins follows Three Commutes with Piano Etudes, Book I, six works of tender wisdom (September 25). On the cover of conditions for observing light, pianist Cephas Azariah seems to have been shot through with a sunbeam. The metaphor applies to the composer’s work, which also touches on ambient and electronic territory, while searching fro radiance in all of its forms (Anjunachill, September 3). With radiant contributions from Clarice Jensen and Spencer Zahn, Sova (Sophia Vastek) can do no wrong. As one might expect from the title, early single “Heavy Shit” is an exercise in darkness, but the album Alight! is a study of contrasts, anchored by Sova’s exquisite keys (Hout, September 4). Double bass and electronics merge on Fragments, an album long in the making; Fragment I debuted in 2025. By blending genres, ZKHR hopes to appeal to multiple audiences (September 19).   Dobrinka Tabakova has been accumulating the pieces of Stone Trail for nearly a quarter-century; now they are gathered in one place. The album is graced with numerous collaborators, and is one of our furthest-out releases, dropping November 13 on NMC. The first half of Episodic Memory includes a murder ballad, but the second is a vibrant instrumental suite that comments on the experience of trauma. Exceptet and Bendon Randall-Myers handle both with aplomb (cmntx, October 9). Daniella Ljungsberg splits Other Plans between vocal and instrumental pieces, but when she sings, she does so with reverence, honoring the Baroque nature of these tender Nordic folk tales (ORTHODOX, October 2). Alfredo Ovalles and Black Page Orchestra present The Art of Parties on September 18, preceded by the inviting single Dance! (PARMA). Richard Allen

items.body: Solythode maintains an unrelenting presence, often opening​ with uneasy ambient-noise structures before expanding toward the outer edges of mechanical rhythms and threaded bass lines that seem to operate just outside our galaxy. Industrial braindance and fractured electronic textures Solythode by Cathopsis   Their initial self-titled collaboration, tagged as “a seriously tough and targeted collection of harsher electronics” in 2023, seared through dense soundscapes. Their latest effort, titled Solythode—yet another spoonerism—sees both Cathode Ray Tube (CRT, aka Chang Terhune) and Solypsis (aka James Miller) working through ten tracks of industrial braindance and fractured electronic textures. A hardened The JD’s-styled synth-breakbeat pulse drives opener “Planet Downer,” while melodic blips and bleeps in “Plague Zone” push Cathopsis’ tone toward soundtrack-like passages and clustered crevasses, eventually locking into heavier techno-industrial thuds midway through. Dub-infested glitch elements cut through “Ghilie Suit Dub,” where broken beats form a dysfunctional whole, with an illbient power-noise sheen pushing the track forward into increasingly distorted territory. A serious powerhouse. Solythode maintains an unrelenting presence, often opening​ with uneasy ambient-noise structures before expanding toward the outer edges of mechanical rhythms and threaded bass lines that seem to operate just outside our galaxy. “Chrome Under Dark” stands out, its technoid undercurrent tempered just enough to keep ears and attention fixed on what might emerge next. Closing pieces, including the thudding ultra-bass march of “Chyron Prophet” and the crepuscular broken rhythm of “New Dreams,” make it clear that both Terhune and Miller are comfortable generating momentum from darkness. Working from opposing sides of an un-United States, Solythode is another mind-bending collection of hard-edged electronic and industrial IDM material, well suited to carrying us through increasingly treacherous times. Fans of Displacer, Xanopticon, Orphx, and Antigen Shift should take notice. Solythode is available on Component. items.body: Philippe Blache has constructed a detailed sonic environment where piano, electronics, repetition, and shifting textures create a sustained feeling of uncertainty, contemplation, and spectral loss. Liminal spaces, paramnesia, and the elusive nature of affective memory Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind by Philippe Blache   Philippe Blache‘s work has long occupied a fascinating space where neoclassical composition, dark electronics, and carefully sculpted atmosphere intersect. On Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind, his latest release for Bulgaria’s Mahorka label, those elements come together in a particularly compelling form. It is a dark and moody album, but there is considerably more happening beneath its somber surface. Blache has constructed a detailed sonic environment where piano, electronics, repetition, and shifting textures create a sustained feeling of uncertainty, contemplation, and spectral loss. The album’s conceptual foundation explores liminal spaces, paramnesia, and the elusive nature of affective memory. Those ideas are present in the music without requiring the listener to approach the album as a literal narrative. Instead, Blache translates them into sound. The pieces seem to occupy spaces that are recognizable but somehow altered, places where familiar structures have become unstable. There is a ​persistent sensation of movement without a clear destination, as though the music is wandering through an environment that exists just outside ordinary perception. Blache is perhaps best known as the mastermind behind the long-running neoclassical dark ambient project Day Before Us, and there is an obvious continuity between that work and this solo release. Yet Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind feels distinct in its approach. The piano is especially important, providing occasional points of definition within the more fluid electronic material. Rather than functioning simply as a melodic centerpiece, the piano often feels like another texture within the larger architecture. Its presence can suggest something intimate and human, while the surrounding electronics introduce ambiguity and distance. That contrast is one of the album’s greatest strengths. Blache understands how effectively a relatively simple acoustic sound can be transformed when placed inside an electronic environment. Piano tones linger within layers of sustained sound, while subtle shifts in timbre and density continually reshape the space around them. The result is music that can feel simultaneously close and remote. “Blache creates tension through accumulation and repetition. A tone may initially seem almost static, only to reveal small internal movements as the piece progresses. These details encourage attentive listening and give the album a considerable amount of depth.” ~Don Haugen The electronic textures are particularly impressive. There is a strong sense of patience in the way sounds are allowed to develop, overlap, and gradually change. Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Blache creates tension through accumulation and repetition. A tone may initially seem almost static, only to reveal small internal movements as the piece progresses. These details encourage attentive listening and give the album a considerable amount of depth. There is also something wonderfully spectral about Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind. Its sounds frequently seem to exist between states, neither entirely present nor completely disappearing. This quality connects beautifully with the album’s exploration of liminal spaces and shifting memories. Blache creates the sensation of something that is almost remembered, something felt at the edges of consciousness but never completely recovered. The album’s melancholia is therefore not simply a matter of dark tones or minor-key piano. It is embedded in the structure of the compositions themselves. Repetition becomes important here, with recurring elements gradually taking on different emotional meanings as their surroundings change. A phrase or texture that initially feels stable can become unsettling when it returns in a slightly altered context. An intriguing and beautifully constructed work :: The collaboration with photographer and visual storyteller objet-fantôme, Angela Caro, also reinforces the album’s interest in unusual psychological and spatial environments. The music and visual concept share an appreciation for ambiguity, allowing the listener to inhabit an imagined territory rather than simply observe it from a distance. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is an intriguing and beautifully constructed work. Its darkness is balanced by subtle beauty, its electronic textures are remarkably detailed, and its use of piano gives the album a welcome emotional anchor. Most importantly, Blache understands the value of restraint. The music does not need to announce its intentions. It gradually reveals them. This is an album that rewards repeated listening, with new details emerging from its carefully layered surfaces. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is an atmospheric and thoughtfully realized excursion into uncertainty, melancholia, repetition, and the spaces between what we experience and what we can fully understand. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is available on Mahorka. items.body: DiN has built an extensive catalog through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. The realization of a conversation that required time to develop Juxtapositions (DiN97) by Boddy | Scanner   Collaboration can be a particularly revealing form of musical exchange. When two artists with long-established identities enter the same creative space, the result can either reinforce familiar strengths or uncover previously unexplored territory. On Juxtapositions, Ian Boddy and Scanner, the recording identity of Robin Rimbaud, accomplish the latter with remarkable assurance. Both are legendary figures within the broad landscape of electronic music, yet they approach sound from distinctly different perspectives. That contrast becomes the central strength of this nine-track collaboration. Released on Boddy‘s long-running DiN imprint, Juxtapositions brings together two musicians whose individual careers have been defined by curiosity, exploration, and an ability to continually expand their respective vocabularies. Scanner has previously appeared on DiN through his solo releases An Ascent and The Homeland of Electricity, while his work alongside Boddy at Manchester’s Subliminal Impulse festival ​in 2022 offered an earlier indication of what their musical connection might produce. Four years later, Juxtapositions feels less like a casual meeting of established artists and more like the realization of a conversation that required time to develop.   Fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details :: The album’s title is particularly appropriate. Boddy and Rimbaud‘s approaches remain identifiable, but neither musician simply occupies a separate half of the sound field. Instead, their contrasting methods continually intersect and reshape one another. Cycling electronic patterns emerge and gradually lose their boundaries within more diffuse textures. Carefully articulated sequences create a sense of forward movement before dissolving into reverberant spaces filled with fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details. The opening “Exclusion Zone” immediately establishes this sense of unstable balance. Repetition and atmosphere coexist without either becoming dominant, creating a piece that seems simultaneously structured and unsettled. The duo understands the expressive potential of restraint. Ideas are allowed to develop gradually, and changes in texture or emphasis often arrive so naturally that the listener may only recognize the transformation after it has already occurred. “A Passing Trace” continues this approach with an appropriately elusive quality, while “Voltage in Bloom” introduces a more energized sense of motion. Throughout the album, Boddy‘s sensitivity to melodic and sequential development provides an important sense of internal architecture, while Scanner‘s interventions introduce ambiguity, disruption, and a fascination with the physical and accidental characteristics of sound. The combination is particularly effective because neither artist appears interested in forcing a stylistic compromise. “Sotto Voce” explores quieter territory, allowing subtle shifts in tone and atmosphere to carry much of the composition’s emotional weight. This is followed by “Intersignals,” where fragments of communication and electronic activity become part of the musical environment. Scanner‘s recognizable use of radio transmissions and found audio is particularly effective throughout Juxtapositions. These elements never feel like decorative references or conceptual interruptions. Instead, they introduce a human presence that is distant, fragmented, and often impossible to fully understand. Source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate :: That tension between familiarity and abstraction becomes increasingly important as the album progresses. Field recordings from old houses and reverberant cellars suggest physical spaces without reducing them to easily identifiable locations. They become acoustic environments within the compositions, their resonances and imperfections blending with synthesized sound until distinctions between source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate. “A Room of Hammers” is among the album’s most evocative titles and its slightly extended duration allows the duo to explore a particularly rich interplay between texture, resonance, and implied physicality. Sounds seem to occupy depth rather than simply appearing across the stereo field. There is a strong sense of entering spaces within the music, each one containing its own acoustic characteristics and hidden activity. The final third of the album demonstrates how successfully Boddy and Scanner have established a shared language. “Shared Frequencies” is perhaps the most fitting title in this respect, suggesting not merely collaboration but communication through common ground discovered in the process of making the music. “Mnemonic Patterns” returns to the album’s interest in repetition and evolving structures, while “A Fleeting Glimpse” brings Juxtapositions to a close without imposing a conventional sense of resolution. This album’s most compelling moments are often found in the details: a pattern that changes almost imperceptibly, a distant tone entering and disappearing, a reverberation suggesting an unexpected depth, or a texture gradually assuming a different character. Two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities :: What makes Juxtapositions especially successful is that it avoids the temptation to present collaboration as a competition between recognizable styles. Boddy and Rimbaud bring their histories and individual sensibilities into the project, but the resulting music belongs to neither artist alone. Their differences become productive points of tension, generating compositions that move between hypnotic repetition, abstract sound design, emotional resonance, and carefully constructed electronic space. DiN has built an extensive catalog through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. For listeners familiar with either artist, Juxtapositions offers the pleasure of hearing two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities through their interaction. For those encountering their work for the first time, it is an absorbing entry point into the creative worlds of both Boddy and Scanner. More importantly, it stands on its own as a deeply considered and beautifully constructed electronic work, one whose subtle movement and hidden detail encourage repeated listening. Juxtapositions is an album about the productive possibilities of difference. Ian Boddy and Robin Rimbaud do not erase the distance between their individual sound worlds. They explore it. Within that space between their approaches, they have created something rich, patient, mysterious, and quietly compelling. Juxtapositions is available on DiN. This is synthetic music realized on synths so people generally like it or hate it. The synthesizer is a marvelous invention and it can generate wave forms based on parameters put into the patch. When it comes close to acoustic sound waves, it has the most warmth and soul. The problem is that the overtones in synthetic sound production will never come close to the complex overtones of an acoustic instrument. However, these musicians know how to manipulate sound and they give it a funkiness and beat that makes it very enjoyable.

items.body: Some artists move between genres as tourists, collecting a new set of surfaces with every release. Kontravoid moves differently. Across skeletal coldwave, heavy EBM, freestyle-informed electro, industrial club music, and dark pop, Cameron Findlay has maintained a character that can be recognized within seconds: disciplined drums, bass that seems to alter the air pressure, synthesizers suspended between metallic seduction and industrial alarm, and an abrasive baritone that sounds transmitted from a sealed room. That consistency amid constant movement has made Kontravoid one of the most important acts in the international darkwave and EBM scene. The Canadian-born, Los Angeles-based musician, drummer, and producer has announced a new full-length album, Sound of the Void, due October 2, 2026, through Toronto’s Artoffact Records. It will be his second album for Artoffact, coming more than two years after his previous release, Detachment, which came out on March 1, 2024. The announcement includes the new single “Without,” joining January’s “Mortal” as the second track available ahead of the album. The space between albums has hardly been empty. Findlay carried Detachment through Europe and North America, appearing at Wave-Gotik-Treffen and playing dates alongside Buzz Kull and Cold Cave. In December 2024, Losing Game Remixes returned to his collaboration with Nuovo Testamento vocalist Chelsey Crowley, while Crowley’s band Nuovo Testamento, Normal Bias, Auragraph, and Tassel each pulled the song into a different corner of the club. Findlay also continued his parallel life as a remixer, recasting Ekko the Strange’s “Reanimate,” Modern English’s “Not My Leader,” Mareux’s “The Perfect Girl,” Buzz Kull’s “In the Cut,” and Raudiver’s “No Sun Rising.” The list stretches from foundational British post-punk to contemporary dark pop, but each rework retains his familiar low-end physicality and severe rhythmic control. That versatility reaches back beyond the mask. Before launching Kontravoid in 2012, Findlay co-founded the Toronto synthpop group Parallels and played drums with Crystal Castles and TR/ST. Kontravoid gave those experiences a single, durable identity, allowing him to change tempo, density, and genre without losing the tension at the center of his music. Findlay’s forthcoming album, Sound of the Void, promises to seamlessly blend coldwave textures with thunderous EBM basslines and pulsating electro rhythms, elevating the body-focused electronic style that has characterized Kontravoid’s recent releases. Yet, “Without” hints that the album will transcend mere repetition of Detachment. The new single “Without” opens on a throbbing bass synthesizer, an alarm-like synthwave figure, and drums pressing forward in precise, heavy strokes. Findlay delivers clipped poetic lines through a harsh vocal treatment as warped synthesizers bend around him. When the verse breaks apart, his voice gives way to a flood of effects surrounding a series of shouts. Dark pads, driving electro rhythms, and lush basslines gather into a cold, nearly solid wall of sound, pulling the track toward something disembodied and otherworldly. The song sits outside any single darkwave, EBM, or coldwave designation, though every pressure point bears Kontravoid’s signature. It is a different kind of Kontravoid track, and a clear example of Findlay operating at the top of his game: widening the project’s vocabulary while keeping its identity intact. Listen to “Without” below and pre-order Sound of the Void here. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Sound of the Void was produced by Findlay and mixed and mastered by Ewan A. Kay. Dylan Frankland contributed live drums to “Without” and closing track “Phantom,” with Daryl Dee handling the live-drum engineering. Jean Lorenzo designed the cover, while Los Angeles photographer Corinne Schiavone, also known as Perpetual Mobile, supplied the original insert photograph. The ten-track album will be available digitally, on CD, and on clear vinyl. A limited black-vinyl test pressing with white labels is also available. The digital edition and CD arrive October 2, while the first vinyl pressing is expected to ship around November 20. Digital preorders include immediate downloads of “Without” and “Mortal.” The album received funding support from FACTOR, the Government of Canada, and Canadian private radio broadcasters. The run begins September 10 at Elysium in Austin and concludes October 24 at the SUBSTANCE festival in Los Angeles. The October 2 album release falls on the tour’s Kansas City stop. Spike Hellis and Normal Bias will join the bill in Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. Tickets and further information are available through Kontravoid’s official website.
