items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,

rhythms, and accordion-based

For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的新作《Langs》延续了前作对外探索的脉络，但姿态更贴近地面。乐队以高音萨克斯为主奏，搭配低音提琴、鼓、模块合成器与电颤琴，开篇曲《Springleik》取材自挪威西部的springleik舞曲。旋律先由萨克斯呈现，随后低音提琴以齐奏方式加入，合成器和电颤琴在背景中添色，角色分工不断流动，整体趋向即兴化。作品在传统民间素材与爵士乐的自由精神之间建立对话，电子声响的融入也提供了当代质感，使熟悉的旋律获得新的展开空间。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items._cn_summary: 这是一份以芝加哥南区街头为背景的声音档案，记录了二十五位受枪击暴力影响的普通人的即兴讲述与自由说唱。制作人Ian Brennan未添加任何音乐，仅保留环境声与呼吸般的现场质感，让话语本身成为叙事主体。录音地点位于祖母门廊前，飞机航道之下，蚊虫与街声交织，强化了纪实性的沉浸感。参与者的年龄从十七岁到六十七岁不等，有人刚刚离开追悼会，有人正要去参加，那些犹豫与崩溃的瞬间比刻意的讲述更富冲击力。项目收益捐赠给Cure Violence Global，使艺术行动与社会议题直接相连。它并非传统意义上的音乐专辑，而是以原始声响记录社区创伤、韧性与被遗忘的日常，具备强烈的实验性与人文厚度。

The last article in our Fall Music Preview includes American Primitive, chamber rock, post-metal and prog, with a little bit of folk and jazz thrown in for good measure. Already we’ve covered hundreds of releases, far too many to fit in our daily review section. As fall is the biggest release season for music, we expect the rapid pace of announcements to continue over the next few months. Be sure to visit our Upcoming Releases page as more titles are added daily! Our cover image comes from Kukangendai‘s Baquet Wheel, covered below. Philadelphia’s Hour continues to be the spiritual successor to Rachel’s. Blending chamber arrangements with a post-rock sensibility, the ever-morphing ensemble straddles genres and exudes a sense of elegance. Ghost Bridge is Hour’s first studio album since 2024’s Ease the Work, and contains moments both intimate and immense (Dear Life, October 9). Stepping out from his Blue Lake moniker, Jason Dungen teams up with Johan Carøe for Routine, which operates as a tribute to domestic life. The album feels like family and home, refuge and safety (Tonal Union, September 25).   We might call HUG a supergroup, as it is comprised of Devendra Banhart, Gyan Riley and Noah Georgeson. The guitar work is intricate and instinctive, and in lead single “Cow With Half Moon Passed,” one can even hear the evening frogs singing along (Luaka Bop, September 11). Twenty years into their career, Kyoto’s Kukangendai is still going strong. Recorded live, Baquet Wheel is an acoustic adventure rife with experimentation and a sense of fun (Marionette, October 4). Bass flute and Moog is a rare combination, owned by Big Bend + a&h on their new album Cloudshaped. The title is fitting, as these amorphous pieces twist and turn, dissolve and reform. Piano, strings, sax, bowed psaltery and more play supporting roles (Dead Currencies, September 25).   While Light Conductor‘s music is often described as “cosmic drone,” we feel it fits more in the categories of rock and folk. This is not to say that the former tag is a misnomer, as both elements are present. Sequence Three is the concluding chapter of a triptych, and is one of three records being released by Constellation on September 25. Oren Ambarchi‘s Cooked isn’t just about the guitar; shō, gamelan and a host of other instruments come into play, thanks to a host of guest stars. With one track per side, the compositions have a copious amount of room (Drag City, September 25). Bhajan Bhoy returns with Electrisol, a shimmering guitar set preceded by the single Palidena, which was originally included on a benefit compilation (Feeding Tube/Cardinal Fuzz). RYMDEN looks an awful lot like Kraftwerk on the Bandcamp page for Today May Be Tomorrow. Their sound incorporates jazz, groove, prog and krautrock, lively and loose (Jazzland recordings Norway, September 25). Midway between Acoustic Ladyland and Melt Yourself Down is Pete Wareham’s lost album with Silver Birch, a blast of punk energy, rhythmic improv and fresh saxophone air. After 15 years, High on the Western Hill still sounds new (Kit, November 13).   Lummernikt is an intricate acoustic guitar album, named after the spores of plants once used for theatrical pyrotechnics. The title might also be applied to the music, which flows like a summer river until it reaches the rapids. Finn Loxbo‘s track titles also have intriguing explanations, with references to poetry, prose, nature and children’s toys (Fönstret, September 18). Half of Mountains returns with Nightlife, demonstrating a surprising jazz bent rather than the expected drone. Koen Holtkamp introduces the set with the hypnotic video for “Slow Fox Run.”(Western Vinyl, October 9). We normally find Hausu Mountain in our Electronic section, but Crying Laughing‘s Talking is a different animal: a jazz and funk-laden excursion with healthy doses of percussion (including cowbell!), alto sax and “Ricemeat” (September 10). Eiderdown Records started the season early, releasing two new albums yesterday. Nick Jonah Davis‘ Rose Delta Rising lies on the border of post-rock, gentle and kind, but with upbeat numbers like “Poa Kichizi” to get the crowds dancing. Steven R. Smith‘s Half Light Unfolding operates in a similar tonal range, with guitar, piano and organ, an intimate set that calms the heart and warms the spirit. For a discount, purchase as a pair!   Allison De Groot‘s clawhammer banjo meets Rich Ruth‘s diverse instrumentation on their self-titled LP, whose tones range from lullaby to campfire stomp, with electronic surprises in-between. “10-14” is our favorite (Western Vinyl, October 2). Davide Cedolin follows his Ligurian Pastoral series with Cjera Aʃìn, which is informed by the artist’s “origin land” of Val d’Arzino in Northern Italy. Graced by field recordings from the region, the album is a mix of American primitive, folk and drone, and has a homespun, deep woods tone, perfect for its release on the precipice of the autumnal equinox (September 21). Debacle Records is the new home for Verdin Brothers, who combine field recordings, bluegrass and hauntology on The Crooked Serpent, a collection of late night tales told by a crackling fire (October 16).   What’s on your Dance Card? Adam Hill‘s album includes modern composition and pedal steel!). With seven different composers and a decet, the surprises keep coming, while the fascination level remains high (September 18). The Mexican guitar duo Rodrigo y Gabriela makes a joyful noise with pieces inspired by “rogue monsters, celestial birds and other fantastical creatures.” On one track they become a trio, but OurHome sounds like the work of a quartet (ATO, September 18). Hannes Kretzer‘s music lurks before it pounces, catching listeners off guard like helpless prey. The intensely cinematic Amor Fati sounds like the work of a full band, especially at the rocking end of tracks such as “Devotion & Decay.” Recorded in a 16th century castle church, the album includes guest vocals from Vargkvint and may inspire listeners to develop their own narratives (September 25). Shipwreck Orchestra is not actually an orchestra, but it may as well be, since frontman Aaron Miller plays over a dozen instruments, enhanced by the contributions of a small number of friends. On Papers Relating to an Unattributed Journal, participants use 19th century instruments to weave a conceptual tale (September 11). From the title and artist name, we knew that Glorious 70mm‘s Death Is for Mortals No Longer an Evil, But a Blessing was a pure post-rock album. What we couldn’t tell was that it was a solo effort: immense in sound, difficult to bring on tour. The sound seems tailor-made for silent film scoring, reflecting the wise moniker (September 4). On the same day, Northampton post-rock quartet AV Sunset releases Vs Reality, whose sequences of sweetness are balanced by cathartic explosions, demonstrated in the center of “The Cheerleading Elite” (September 4).   The sound of Edmonton’s Pigeon Breeders lies somewhere between post-rock and noise rock; Springtime as Violence, justifies its title with subtle distortion and thick surges of sound (Honey Farm, September 4). Collapse Under the Empire’s Chris Burda steps out on his own as Age of Life, unveiling the ambitious, cinematic Emergence – Part I. Each track corresponds to a unique era of evolutionary time (CB, October 30). Swiss post-prog rockers hubris. are already on their fifth album, preceded by the Tolkien-inspired single “Death.” White Shores is out September 10. Want even heavier stuff? Try Ølyp, whose energetic progressive metal is enhanced by viola, violin and cello, the sugar to their salt. I(m)MORAL is available on sunshine splatter vinyl and preceded by the head-banging The Human Error (Klonosphere, September 25). Ovoo (not to be confused with OvO) unleashes Obsidian on October 2, with blasts of guitar fury so powerful they blow the top off the mountain, as seen on the cover. Spoken word passages only add to the drama. We hope that you’ve enjoyed our Fall Music Preview and that we’ve given you plenty to look forward to! Richard Allen

items.body: LEENALCHI restage a moment from Korean court speech in “Crying Softshell Turtle.” 별주부가 울며 여짜오되 is the narrator’s cue, spoken in the deeply honorific register a subject uses addressing a king: “Officer Turtle, weeping, humbly says to the king.” It repeats three times across the lyrics, each time introducing a new plea from a soldier turtle on his knees before the Dragon King, begging to cut open a captured rabbit’s belly before the animal talks its way out of the trap. LEENALCHI is a seven-piece band from Seoul, four pansori-trained singers fronting two bassists and a drummer. Park Soo Bum, Choi Su In, Ra Seo Jin and Ahn Yi Ho carry the story’s different voices and its narration between them, while bassists Jang Young Gyu and Ejae lock into drummer Oh Hyung Suk‘s groove underneath. That groove tightens hard on the KCRW session. Midway through the track, the two basses drive into a punk-edged instrumental break that sharpens the standoff between the turtle’s frantic pleading and the rabbit’s swagger, and the singers trade lines rather than harmonise over it, snapping into pansori’s guttural, high-pitched delivery to voice each character as the scene turns. The rabbit gets the last word, daring them to open him up: “You will find nothing but dung.” The song comes from Sugungga, an 18th-century pansori epic about a Dragon King who can only be cured by a rabbit’s liver and the turtle sent to fetch it, and LEENALCHI built their 2020 album of the same name by stripping that centuries-old sung narration down to bass, drums and voice. Bassist Jang Young Gyu leads the band and has also scored the films The Wailing and Train to Busan, and this year has been a busy one under his watch: LEENALCHI signed to Luaka Bop, released the EP Here Comes That Crow in June, and will finally put Sugungga out worldwide on 2 October. The release opens a fall tour that runs through the US before crossing into Europe in mid-November, with UK dates in Dublin, London, Bristol, Leeds and Manchester closing out the run. items.body: This is electro with its lineage intact and its eyes firmly ahead: studied, physical, detailed and properly funky. The lesson is simple. Know the form. Then push the production until the form starts pushing back. The roots of electro remain completely visible Interior Reset by Fleck E.S.C.   Committed electrologist Fleck E.S.C. brings his archetypal electro to legendary second-generation post-pioneer, pioneer ADJ’s Pyramid Transmissions for a full album workout as Interior Reset. What’s striking is how the roots of electro remain completely visible without ever collapsing into routine, lazy aesthetics or genre confirmation. These tracks are meticulously built, every texture and hi-hat seemingly calibrated to extract the maximum nuance from the intention. “Interior Reset” is the proof. Broken-tech funk, breakery and serious synthesis craft merge into something that feels both timestamped and timeless. It recalls the impact of seminal rarities that is the Scopex 12”s in the late ’90s (look ’em up), or later on Plaid with “Tether,” and the peerless LA Synthesis “Harmonic Disassembly:” the kind of electro you could play to an enquiring alien who asks, “So, what is electro?” Humanity would be doing itself a solid by choosing those and these. Rarified space devoid of cluttered copycat air. Elsewhere, “Technical Support” drips with grandeur and funk, groove-heavy and boldly beautiful, while “Cyclopedia” comes on like a link-friendly throwdown: body-popping, bone-shaking electro with enough technical muscle to make the point without ever showing off. This is production as practice, not display. Every move has purpose. Nothing is there simply because electro says it should be. “Opalissism” brings weight and width, its staccato arpeggios and spray-gun beats flickering across the stereo field, before “Interior Reset” opens the floor beneath the whole thing, using negative space and broken digi-breaks to let the darker pressure breathe. Then the full eight-minute version of the album’s primary cut arrives, beefed-up and beautifully unruly, all prime-time beats and synthetic muscle. “Moon Landing” follows with swell, swagger and synths jostling for dominance before the drums finally kick the door in. And then “Realisation Roads” takes the closing position and absolutely earns it. Fleck E.S.C., aka Franck Collin, goes hard and home, bringing the record down on a final surge of propulsion and precision. The album leaves the impression of an artist who knows the history intimately but has no interest in living inside it. This is electro with its lineage intact and its eyes firmly ahead: studied, physical, detailed and properly funky. The lesson is simple. Know the form. Then push the production until the form starts pushing back. Faultless electro. Not predictable but familiar enough to be easy to grasp. Interior Rest is genuinely stunning. items.body: Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. A calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes Another World by Artificial Island   London-based duo Artificial Island, lifelong friends Gareth Williams and Ian Prytherch, announce their debut album, Another World, bringing together some of their strongest material from previous releases alongside three new tracks: “Spirit,” “A Different Sun,” and “Departure.” It also includes their most widely recognized track, “Emerge,” a delicate blend of softened synth tones and lullaby-like melodies. All material has been remastered by Guy Davie at Electric Mastering in London, whose credits include Jon Hopkins, Marconi Union and Four Tet. Between cascading ambient-techno archways and ethereal waves of light, Another World generates carefully focused momentum. Traversing Another World, Artificial Island gradually unfolds a calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes, with each track given room to develop through subtle shifts in texture and tone. “After Dark” is built around a floating atmosphere, soft electronic tones and light glitches that drift in and out of focus. “A Different Sun” introduces neo-classical elements, gently moving through cinematic textures and restrained melodic passages, while “Departure” focuses on microscopic details, weaving soft blips and bleeps aro​und low-flying beat pulses and a steady, understated rhythmic strain. As the album moves towards its closing tracks, “Lodestar” returns to spacious, celestial textures, balancing subtle movement with a sense of stillness. Closing piece “Lumen” takes a more distant approach, built from isolated ambient tones, soft electronic whirs and fragments that seem to hover just beyond reach. Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. Built around atmospheric electronics, ambient textures and carefully layered detail, Another World should appeal to fans of Boards of Canada, Marconi Union and Carbon Based Lifeforms. The artwork was designed by Chris Bigg, who spent three decades at 4AD’s legendary v23 design studio alongside Vaughan Oliver, creating artwork for Pixies, Cocteau Twins, Dead Can Dance, The Breeders, and David Sylvian. Bigg has remained David Sylvian’s long-time design collaborator ever since. Another World is self-released on October 2, 2026, available across streaming platforms as well as CD and a limited-edition 2x180g white-vinyl pressing. items.body: The depth and breadth of Documents of Different Reality is truly amazing. Cold Blow have done their homework and their research. This is a compilation of archaeological detail that brings to life the momentous machine music of the 1990s. In Spara’s own words, the collection connects “dots that people might have not connected before.” Turning back the clock and digging into the crates to pay homage to the compilation Documents of Different Reality by Various   Back in the 1990s, the main means of communication for artists and labels happened in record stores. Afficionados and shop owners were the harbingers, acting as a go between for artists, labels and the audience. These gatekeepers would lead the bright eyed to the turntables and hand over a stack of vinyl. Coins jingled and sounds were exchanged. A keystone of finding new music was the compilation. Some imprints dedicated themselves to the format. Others used it to bridge geographical divides and knit together fellow analogue alchemists. Warp Records had Artificial Intelligence, Eevo Lute had Agenda, connections took hold. A glut of tapes filled bedrooms and car stereos as Detroit entered Berlin and Berlin arrived in Sheffield. Cold Blow are turning back the clock and digging into the crates to pay homage to the compilation and the artists who defined a sound and a time. The project is daring and I caught up with Pete Spara of Cold Blow to give some insights into Documents of Different Reality. For those who might not have come across Cold Blow, it’s a London/Helsinki based label with both founders hailing from Finland. Pete Spara, co-founder, describes Cold Blow as an imprint that aims to “release leftfield dance and electronic music often with a bit of a 90s vibe to it. Analog, quirky. Some new stuff, some anthologies, some re-issues, some compilations.” Documents of Different Reality is the boldest outing to date, a “labour of love” that started in 2019 when Halvtrak sent “a demo in 2019 with the title “Documents of Different Reality.”” The title “planted a seed for a compilation” that harked back to those early days of IDM. However, there was a sense that most “newly recorded music” didn’t fit that “very specific sound so the project ended up on the shelf for many years.” But, “the idea was so compelling” that is was “resurrected…as a retrospective.” Although Halvtrak’s “namesake track didn’t end up on the compilation” his contribution is acknowledged…in the liner notes, and he recorded the promo mix for Juno Daily when the release dropped. Technology and the passage of time permeate these Documents. When much of this music was released, there was an optimism of what machines would do for mankind and that we were collectively journeying to a better future. “I wanted people to think about the era when the music was recorded, and the present day, as two different realities. You can hear future-optimism in the music. What might those producers have imagined technology, artificial intelligence and everyday life would look like thirty years later, and how does that compare with the reality we inhabit now?” To connect the original period with a contemporary interpretation of it :: That hopefulness trills from the outset with a sublime example from the Netherlands. 2000 And One & Sandy Huner offer the spine-tingling “Eternal Life.” Nostalgic, yes, but also timeless, this is a beautiful example of ambient techno. Crystalline chords cascade, birdsong swoops above the understated double bass before a beat finally arrives to puncture the lush canopy. Humans are extended into machine in the refrain of “Life Forever” by Mind Control. A track conjured by Syzygy, Dominic Glenn, and Zendik, Justin MacKay, the Infinite Dreams mix first appeared on the UK’s Rumour Records in 1992. Lovingly restored, warm pads and strings are cooled by rasping rhythms as jazzy brass, echoing samples and twinkling notes orbit. The compilation’s focus is on the artists and labels of Europe. Originally, there was a plan to span the continents in search of tracks, but the scope of the project was already quite daunting. “It’s often difficult to reach the artists. There were tracks on the shortlist where even the original label had completely lost contact with the producer.” Searching the East, Cold Blow attempted to track down a “great Japanese track” and hit a dead end with all those involved being “totally disconnected.” Yet, this is part of the story and part of the compilation. The realities have shifted and some have chosen the “refreshing” route of not being absorbed into the sprawling communication networks we now find ourselves rooted in. Thankfully, there is an absolute treasure trove of tracks to choose from across Europe. LA Synthesis, superstars of noodling techno, have been drafted in for the blissfully bangin’ “Positive Negative.” A melody of stardust bends and shifts in a multitude of directions under the steady whomp of a kick. Iceland’s Thor pushes the tempo a little higher with “Break It.” Beat driven, this work melts minimal moments with electro grandeur as the sound of Detroit is reimagined. Methodical in structure, a slow and throbbing groove is peppered with sidesteps of elation. Unsung masters follow. Connective Zone released on A13 in the 1990s, alongside the likes of LA Synthesis and Stasis. More recently, the duo have returned with a number of self-released digital albums. “Electrons” surfaced in 2021 on their DAT Tapes collection. Recorded in 1993, the track is a soundtrack of a dawning future. Sci-fi streaked and immediately immersive, it is elegant and perfectly formed; a window into a seriously talented pair. “The optimism of the 1990s might have been eclipsed by something very different, but in these tracks there remains a poignancy and human touch that still hold the seed of what our reality can be.” ~Robbie Geoghegan Hidden amongst these gleaming gems of yesteryear is a contemporary addition. Barcelona based Permutation with “Atlas.” Spara remembers that “Dmitry & Edgar (Permutation) sent demos” when the compilation was being created. The “influence of the era” was immediate and their involvement allowed the collection “to connect the original period with a contemporary interpretation of it.” Reflective and ruminative, “Atlas” blends the aquatic elements of dub with the astral brightness that characterized the sounds showcased across Documents. Arguably, the most recognisable name on the sleeve is Steve Pickton under his Stasis moniker. Taken from the Inspiration album, which came out on Peacefrog in 1995, “World Out Of Time” is low-slung future funk. From the rattle and rumble of the intro, Pickton takes the listener up and away into a deep and soulful trip. Nothing is overly elaborate, the sparse elements and musicianship combining in harmony. A past name, one that is now gaining more attention, closes. Simon Walley released a burst of music in the mid to late 1990s before receding from the scene. Under his CiM alias he continues to delight audiences with his fragile style of electronics. The piece chosen is “Lead Point” which came out in 1998 on Headspace Recordings. Almost floating, this light and subtle work sails above ruffled rhythms and is a glimpse into the wonderful music of this musician. The depth and breadth of Documents of Different Reality is truly amazing. Cold Blow have done their homework and their research. This is a compilation of archaeological detail that brings to life the momentous machine music of the 1990s. In Spara’s own words, the collection connects “dots that people might have not connected before.” This “labour of love” is a testament to the artists and to Cold Blow. The optimism of the 1990s might have been eclipsed by something very different, but in these tracks there remains a poignancy and human touch that still hold the seed of what our reality can be. Documents of Different Reality is available on Cold Blow. items.body: Review by Hrychu — I managed to get my hands on this rare (Ahoy!) American prog album and I listened to the whole thing. Iliked it. The musical ideas are really cool and they're very competently performed. It's clear thatthe band was going for a quirky Gentle Gianty retro/Canterbury Scene type sound. I think theirimpression is as good as it gets. The vocals in particular really do channel that style to a T. Theprecise and dynamic drumming courtesy of the late Marc Cella recorded with near-period-correctattention to sonic detail elevates the album to another level. There's one element though that Ithink kinda sticks out imo. It's the very obviously digital sounding 90's ROMpler organ and stringsynth parts. When juxtaposed with the genuine M400 Mellotron machine that the band proudly used onthe album, those digital textures are clearly clashing with the vintage ones and it's not really apleasant mixture, I think. On track #7, for instance, right after a pastoral section full of fuzzguitars, Minimoog solos and Mellotron chords, all of the sudden, an awkward snippet of cheesymuzak-y string ensemble sounds straight from a dollar bin Yamaha keyboard comes up. The clonewheelorgan sound isn't all that convincing either. I think its biggest giveaway is the lack of the iconicnote attack/release click that a real tonewheel Hammond organ would always produce. But that's not ahuge deal. My favorite track? Invitation/Pitch the Wort. That one's pure retro prog joy with nofluff.*review originally published in the form of a casual post on progressiveears
