items.body: Skinny Puppy released their second studio album, “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” through Nettwerk on 5 September 1986. The Vancouver industrial band’s sophomore record turns 40 this year. It is the album that introduced keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to the lineup and pushed the group’s sound away from its early synth-pop leanings toward a heavier, sample-driven style. Dave Ogilvie and cEvin Key produced, engineered and mixed the album, which was released on vinyl and cassette through Nettwerk in Canada and the US and through Play It Again Sam in Europe; Capitol Records-EMI handled Canadian distribution, a deal that expanded the record’s retail reach from roughly 200 to 1,700 stores across the country. The cover, a photograph by frequent collaborator Steven R. Gilmore taken from a pornographic film he saw on a hotel television in New York City, later won Best Album Art at the 1987 CASBY Awards and landed the record on one of Tipper Gore’s Parents Music Resource Center lists. A 1988 CD reissue on Capitol Records added four bonus tracks, including the single “Chainsaw,” to the original nine-song lineup. The lead single, “Dig It,” received regular MTV airplay and a Billboard recommendation, and “Stairs and Flowers” followed as a second single; Skinny Puppy toured North America and Europe with Severed Heads to support the release. “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” streams on Bandcamp and is also available on Spotify. Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse by Skinny Puppy About Skinny Puppy Skinny Puppy started in Vancouver, Canada, in 1982 as a side project for drummer cEvin Key (born Kevin Crompton), who was also playing in the new wave band Images in Vogue. Key brought in vocalist Nivek Ogre (Kevin Ogilvie), and the two adopted stage names to tell the two Kevins apart. The pair self-released the “Back & Forth” EP in 1983 and signed to the Vancouver label Nettwerk that same year. A second EP, “Remission,” followed in December 1984, and the debut album, “Bites,” arrived in 1985 with Bill Leeb, performing as Wilhelm Schroeder, on bass synth and backing vocals. Leeb left in 1986 to start Front Line Assembly, and Key hired keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to replace him. Goettel, a classically trained pianist with a background in samplers and the Ensoniq Mirage, had met Key the year before, when his band Water opened for Skinny Puppy. He made his first appearance on record on “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” released 5 September 1986. Key later called Goettel “the master of sampling.” Skinny Puppy went on to release “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988), “Rabies” (1989, featuring Ministry’s Al Jourgensen), “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992), their final album for Nettwerk. In 1993 the band signed to Rick Rubin’s American Recordings and moved to Los Angeles to record “The Process.” Ogre left the band in June 1995, and Goettel died two months later, on 23 August 1995, at the age of 31. Key and producer Dave “Rave” Ogilvie completed “The Process,” releasing it in 1996 in Goettel’s memory. Skinny Puppy reunited for a one-off show in Dresden, Germany, in 2000 and became a full-time act again in 2003 with producer Mark Walk, releasing “The Greater Wrong of the Right” (2004), “Mythmaker” (2007), “HanDover” (2011) and “Weapon” (2013). “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” turns 40 in 2026 as the first Skinny Puppy album to feature Goettel, who remained with the band until his death in 1995.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.

A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — I am not an expert in music, so I cannot always explain exactly what musical techniques create these feelings. 1. Jungle WaltzAn interesting combination of vocals and musical instruments immediately catches attention. There is a bright transition into a denser part, which is then replaced by another mood, more positive and mysterious. The sound feels quite exotic, with a gradual addition of more intensity. As the composition develops, it becomes more epic and mysterious. It feels like entering an unknown world and slowly discovering what is inside it. 2. Meekness and GentlenessVery cheerful, pleasant, and light-hearted. I had an association with the beauty of fast movement. The composition creates a very joyful mood and seems to encourage the listener to move and enjoy life. Despite its somewhat gloomy beginning, it becomes very alive and energetic. It leaves a feeling of happiness and lightness.3. Lavoro d'AmoreThe beginning feels very friendly and welcoming, creating a warm and pleasant mood. Gradually, it changes into a deeper and more noble feeling of love, which seems to fill the whole soul and elevate it to another level. It feels like love requires some difficult work and effort, but after this work is done, peace and harmony finally arrive.4. Be Ye Not UnwiseThe beginning is very gloomy and perhaps reflects the consequences of unwise human behaviour. The listener is surrounded by a very dark and almost hopeless atmosphere. There is a strong feeling of sadness and sorrow, which seems to reflect the horror of human recklessness. At some point, the music creates a feeling of emptiness, as if nothing can be changed anymore.5. Passing OverThe composition has a touching and cozy beginning, which gradually develops into a brighter but still very emotional atmosphere. Then there is a sudden transition back to a more tender feeling. After that, the emotions become much stronger, and the atmosphere grows more intense. It inspires the listener to struggle, work hard, and keep moving forward.Eventually, the tension decreases and the music becomes more peaceful and measured. It feels like a transition from struggle to acceptance and harmony, both with the surrounding world and with oneself.6. PremonitionThe beginning feels like the birth of a certain feeling. The listener seems to be paying attention to very small and almost unnoticeable details. Gradually, this feeling becomes stronger and starts to influence the person. It feels as if someone trusts their intuition, and this gives them a direction for moving forward.Later, the music becomes more brutal and perhaps more confident, almost as if the person becomes sure that they are right. Finally, everything becomes calmer, creating a feeling of satisfaction because the intuition turned out to be correct. The whole composition feels very epic and touching.7. Patience of HopeHope is a very important part of life, especially in our time. The composition begins in a touching way and then moves into a faster tempo, creating an atmosphere of movement and life. It slows down and then accelerates again, which gives the listener energy and inspires them to work and live despite difficulties.Later, the music seems to reach a higher level of immersion. It can be connected with faith that everything will eventually be fine. I like the combination of inspiration and calmness here. It gives strength without creating too much tension. 8. Her LoveA very sweet and energetic beginning reflects strength and hard work. Then the music becomes lighter and more energetic. There is a feeling of sincerity and care, which later can become lost in the difficulties and struggles that appear in relationships.At the same time, there is passion and strong involvement, which can also create complications. However, persistence and the desire to preserve the relationship make it possible to overcome these difficulties. The composition feels like a story about love that is not always easy but is worth making an effort for.9. Through Difficult DecisionsA feeling of warmth and joy fills the soul here, although it does not come without effort. This makes the experience of life more interesting and meaningful. The composition creates a very full and uplifting atmosphere.Perhaps it is also about one's worldview. If a person loves life and remains true to themselves, even difficult decisions may become less difficult to make. There is a feeling that being honest with yourself gives you the strength to move through complicated situations.10. Psalm 6The fast tempo at the beginning seems to represent difficult trials and heavy experiences. Then comes a moment of despair, sadness, and anxiety. However, it feels as if the person realizes that they cannot remain in this state forever and starts searching for hope.This journey is not easy. It requires courage and determination to escape from despair. The composition creates an atmosphere of inner struggle, where courage and strength of spirit are necessary to continue moving forward.I really enjoyed listening to this album. It is the kind of music that ennobles the soul.

items.body: Composer Anthony Davis Anthony Davis has never hesitated to share express his feelings and politics in his music. His operas “X: The Life and Times of Malcolm X” (1986) and “Amistad” (1997) are two recent shining examples. Album Cover This most recent of his operas is also one that partakes of more recent political events than the previously mentioned works. It is, by my count, his 8th opera. And though all of Davis’ operas can be said to have some political content, “X”, “Amistad”, and now “The Central Park Five (2019), are most specifically focused on the transatlantic slave trade (ca. 1500- 1870) and subsequent black political history.. Librettist Richard Wesley The story captured in the libretto by Richard Wesley made newspaper headlines and even motivated the pre presidential Donald Trump to take out full page ad in several media publications advocating their guilt and advocating for the death penalty. Performance photo by JJ Geiger While I have had the pleasure of multiple hearings of this powerful and substantial work I have chosen to include the composer’s excellent essay which describes not only the story but also the some of the intricacies and references embedded in the music itself. Notes on The Central Park Five By Anthony Davis 1989. A group of predominantly Black and Hispanic teenagers enter Central Park in New York City. They turnover garbage cans, throw rocks, harass people on bicycles. A young woman is sexually assaulted in the Park and six teenagers are detained and questioned about the assault. Five of the teenagers, Kevin Richardson, Raymond Santana, Korey Wise, Yusef Salaam and Antron McCray become the center of a criminal case that would polarize New York City. The Exonerated Five were falsely accused and convicted of the crime with no physical evidence. Condemned publicly by the press, the Exonerated Five were victims in a culture war waged against  Black and Hispanic communities.  A politically ambitious real estate mogul condemns the teenagers with a full page add, proclaiming “Bring Back the Death Penalty. Bring Back Our Police!” The persecution of the Central Park Five marks the beginning of Donald Trump’s political career, built on racial animus and the exploitation of the deep rooted racial divide in America.  Why? What accounts for what Johnny Cochran would later famously call, “The rush to judgement.” How could the court trust the coerced “confessions” of the five teenagers? How did we come to this moment that assumed guilt, blindly seeking revenge? What caused the deeply rooted anxiety of White Americans when confronted with Black-Hispanic culture  and people?  1989. Spike Lee’s movie Do the Right Thing premieres, Quincy Jones’ album “Back on the Block” debuts, Black and Hispanic teenagers sing the Tone Loc song “Wild Thing” as they descend on the Park. The song becomes a label in the press as they describe the actions in the Park as “Wilding in the Park.” Did the persecution of the Five represent the White anxiety about Hip Hop entering mainstream American culture? Was the response to the Five a reflection of Tony in the Pizza restaurant smashing Radio Raheem’s boombox? The persecution of the Central Park Five, emblematic of other similar incidents of false accusations of Black and Hispanic men  across the country, demonstrates the devastating consequence of the culture war, as incarceration has become the new slavery. As a composer, I have always been drawn to stories that intersect the political and cultural worlds. My operas, X: The Life and Times of Malcolm X, Amistad, Wakonda’s Dream, Tania and Pancho Rabbit and the Coyote, all explore political moments and movements that are reflected in the dynamic of music. In X, it is the evolution of creative music from the forties to the sixties, a revolutionary movement in music as well as in politics. In Amistad, it is the false balance of the Missouri Compromise and the untenable grounding of America’s birth in both the ideals of Democracy and the original sin of Slavery. In American music one must always understand the irony that slavery created our culture from the advent of the minstrel show to the “Birth of the Cool.” Music can capture the tensions and fissures in our cultural and political life and the hope of something better. Music can allow us to feel the powerful forces at play in our lives, forces that are at once destructive but yet in our cathartic engagement allow us to envision a kind of freedom. The Prologue of The Central Park Five begins with the “Exonerated Five” today as they reflect on the past. The opening cross-fade with the Kurzweil texture signify a fissure, a break, the dark spectre of trauma. Each of the Five recalls the trauma of the past. Librettist Richard Wesley ends the Prologue with poignant simplicity, “They tell us in school how big the world is, but that’s their world. They crushed mine.” Act One introduces a recurring theme and harmony that suggests the past world of Harlem. The lyric, “Harlem, a Black and Tan Fantasy,” of course, suggests Ellington’s Harlem. In fact, before the Masque’s aria, the descending minor 3rd in the baritone saxophone suggests Ellington’s famous Tone Parallel to Harlem from 1949. Ellington describes the descending 3rds that appear throughout the work as signifying and enunciating “Harlem.” The theme is introduced by the Baritone Saxophone and starts as a dirge with variations. The harmony in f minor recalls one of Charles Mingus’ most famous harmonic progressions loosely based on the standard, “You Don’t Know What Love Is,” a ballad made famous by Billie Holiday. The melody is then played by the trombone with a counter-melody inspired by the great Eric Dolphy, played by the Baritone Saxophone and the Bass Clarinet. The theme moves into swing with an iteration by the trumpet. This introduces the Masque’s aria, “Harlem, a Black and Tan Fantasy.” The Masque is a malevolent force in the opera. He is the skeptical reporter, who distrusts Black people. He’s the policeman who arrests and interrogates the five suspects. He is the judge who condemns them. In Act One the five singers become their younger selves, before they arrive in Central Park. They are exuberant and recklessly free as they talk about their lives and aspirations. The music begins in a gamelan inspired texture with a 9 beat pattern in the vibraphone  and right hand of the piano and a 10 beat pattern in the left hand of the piano. This creates a repeating grid of 90 beats. As in my first opera, X, often I try to marry underlying rhythmic structures with dramatic intent. Every 90 beats something new can happen in the music and in the drama. The orchestra slowly reveals the inner harmonic working of the drone against the free flowing lines of the Five boys. The Masque disturbs and interrupts the Five’s music signaled by a series of cascading major thirds that play against the harmony of the drone establishing a 4 against 3 rhythmic tension, as the music evolves “off the grid.” This leads to a new tempo before the Masque proclaims  “They (Black people) are lost!” The opera explores rhythmic tension that is reinforced by the harmony. The Five defiantly sing “This is my world!” and later the anthem “The World is Ours!” The stable harmony of the anthem is eventually disturbed by the building polyrhythms as the Five become more excited culminating in the antiphonal rhythmic interplay between “This is no life. This ain’t living. This ain’t no life!” and “Time to bust out, time to break out, time break out, time to act out” This leads the Five into the Park. In the music, I tried to capture the exhilaration and exuberance of the Five and their illusion of freedom. As they enter the Park, the Five sing, “We are the freaks! We are the freaks who own the night!” The music in the Park is influenced by everything from Parliament Funkadelic to fusion Miles Davis and Jaco Pastorius with Weather Report. The music captures the exuberance and recklessness of the Park that quickly becomes out of control fueled by  groove and funk. Music allows us to see different worlds and to shift perspective. As Kevin and Antron are initially detained we hear the echoes of the Blues and again the stop-time from Black and Tan Fantasy as the Masque declares falsely that “That is the end of that.” The anthem music, when it returns as the Assistant District Attorney and the Masque discuss the assault, becomes a distant, shattered memory. The interrogation scenes feature rhythmically driven music as if an ex-machina force is coercing the Five’s confessions. The words of the Masque and the Assistant D.A. are like weapons. The vocal writing is more angular with shifting harmonic centers emphasizing speech rhythms and repetition as the Masque and A.D.A, try to force the Five to implicate each other. This is in contrast with more reflective moments that are lyrical and harmonically grounded. The Five’s collective sense of apprehension and fear is expressed in passages drawn from the vocal ensemble tradition of close harmony from doo-wop, Motown and the street as if through a filter of Gil Evans’ arrangements in “My Ship” or Blues for Pablo. The hybridity of the music tells the story. A friend once asked me, “How do you write for Donald Trump?” I replied, “First, he is a tenor. Second, he repeats himself in his violent sound bytes. Third, he never completes a sentence.” I tried to capture his use of short, repeating phrases that could be amplified by the chorus. “Wilding, Rampaging, Wilding, Rampaging Wolfpack!” What is Trump’s appeal? Like moths to flame, Trump says things that people may think and be afraid to express. In MAGA world Trump’s racism is somehow authentic and Trump has helped unleash the pathological racism that is both systemic and psychological.  I entertained these scary thoughts as I composed the opera. Finally, the opera is an uplifting story of a community rising up against injustice, of the Five finally finding exoneration and vindication as the anthem returns with “The World is Ours!” But we know the cost, as Korey says, “They stole from me!” And we know this is a continuing story. The forces that implicated the Five are still with us. Thank you to the librettist Richard Wesley who illuminated their story with humanity and emotion from Sheronne Salaam’s “They are trying to blame my son” to Korey’s “They stole from me.” None of this would happen without the love and support of my muse, Cynthia Aaronson-Davisuch passionate command. I must recognize the extraordinary work of Earl Howard who created the electro-acoustic world that shadows the opera. I need to call attention to the critical work of Andreas Mitisek who directed the first production in Long Beach and helped realize the dramatic possibilities of the opera. I am indebted to all the musicians and singers who brought this opera to life in Long Beach, Portland and Detroit and, of course, Long Beach Opera, particularly Jenny Rivera and Michelle Magaldi, who believed in the work and help produce this recording. I would also like to thank UCSD for its continued support of my work. None of this would happen without the love and support of my muse, Cynthia Aaronson-Davis. Another performance photo by JJ Geiger The opera has received many performances since its premiere by The Long Beach Opera, who commissioned the work. It has since been performed in Detroit, New York, and is scheduled for another performance in Long Beach. The music incorporates bebop and other jazz styles into a listener friendly melodic and harmonic constructions that set the beautiful libretto’s words effectively. Davis himself identifies as a politically expressive composer. Even in his non-stage works like his meditation on the first of the so called Miranda Rights (You have the right to remain silent) cast in the classical form of a concerto for clarinet (2007). Arguably, Davis’ work cannot be separated from the experience of Black American culture. Davis, raised in the cultural lineage of transgressional innovators such as George Lewis and his many colleagues of the AACM (American Association of Creative Musicians), a group that still works to include the cultures and rituals of many African countries into the practice of so called western art music). Davis has been a defining figure in contemporary music since at least the 1970s. And now he is recognized as an exemplar of “American” music by virtue of the recognition of the Pulitzer Prize. As a work of classical protest music, it functions (in Jeremy Eichler’s term) as “times echo”, a use of great art to frame a noxious historical event in a sort of time capsule that preserves memories and feelings of the story that lives again in performance. As such, The Central Park Five stands proudly alongside Hans Werner Henze’s “Essay on Pigs” (1968), Benjamin Britten’s “War Requiem” (1961), and composers as diverse as Dmitri Shostakovich, Luigi Nono, Arnold Schoenberg, Steve Reich, Wynton Marsalis, and Louis Andriessen (to name but a few). But, as is the case with any artistic work of protest, the actual impact remains to be seen. The horrors of racism remain a defining part of western culture, of American culture now cast forever in this deeply felt drama. This is definitely not, in Toni Morrison’s phrase, “…music to entertain the master and soothe his blunted soul.” And in a time of the active attempts to suppress and deny this unsavory history, art can preserve memories both good and bad.. There is a noble beauty in that.

items.body: Kregel is a Belgian band from Limburg that formed in 2016. Looking for a short, punchy name, they settled on Kregel—a word that suggests stubbornness, contrariness, and, above all, a refusal to submit. While they describe themselves as a Rock band, that label feels somewhat too broad, as their influences clearly lean towards Post-Punk and New-Wave. One of Kregel’s defining characteristics is that they sing in their native language, Dutch. Their lyrics are personal yet compelling, tackling serious subjects with a touch of humor and a rich sense of imagery. Influences such as Aroma Di Amore are never far away, and listeners will inevitably notice the connection with this important touchstone of the Belgian underground scene. However, Kregel is certainly no cheap imitation; they have developed a distinctive sound and personality of their own. Kregel is an idiosyncratic trio with a strong DIY ethos, a mindset that has resulted in a remarkable discography comprising seven EPs to date. Simply numbered “#1” through “#7”, each release features four exclusive tracks. Their latest EP, “#7”, released on Wagonmaniac Music, is another triumph and the direct inspiration for this interview with Bart Timmermans, Sven Derwa, and Jeroen De Smet. Kregel: a musical treasure from Belgium that has so far remained largely hidden from the rest of the world… (Picture credits by BV Fotografisch Atelier Paul Delaet / Interview courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: If I’m not mistaken, Kregel was founded 10 years ago and has released around seven EPs to date. You are gradually making a name for yourselves in the Flemish underground scene, but to an international audience, you still remain somewhat like ‘aliens’. How would you best introduce Kregel to a wider international audience through your key achievements, influences, and future prospects? Sven: Kregel has been around for about 10 years now. We are a Rock trio consisting of Bart (also frontman of both Vandal X and Flipo Mancini) on vocals, drum and bass programming, and occasional keyboards, while Jeroen and I play guitar. Jeroen: We have been playing together since 2008. At first, we were a quintet (Feetfetish), with Bart playing bass. After the departure of the last/10th drummer, we became a quartet (‘Salk). In 2016, our singer had had enough, Bart took over on vocals, and Kregel was born in its current form. Bart: The best introduction to Kregel can be found on the streaming services, where our tracks are available. What you hear there is Kregel. Presenting ourselves to an international audience is a little more difficult because our lyrics are written in Dutch, and they are just as much a defining part of a Kregel song as the music itself. We would not call ourselves ‘aliens’: we are three friends who have been meeting in a rehearsal basement more or less every week for about 15 years, working on our songs and getting a lot of happiness out of it. Sven: That does not mean our music is necessarily a celebration of happiness and joy, because we write songs about our personal concerns and social issues, and unfortunately, it is not all sunshine and roses… Bart: Apart from the seven EPs we have released so far, there are not many other achievements that would make a huge impression on an international audience. Two notable exceptions are the two support slots we played for P.I.L. in May this year (Mr. Lydon is, after all, the godfather of us all; so we guess all of your readers know him), which received a lot of positive reactions. Jeroen: We should also mention our two ‘international tours’. In 2023, we were invited by the John Peel Centre for Creative Arts in England to play a concert, and we added a pub show in London to the trip. Last autumn, we were invited by Mekanic Bird, a kindred-spirit band from Saint-Omer in northern France, to spend a weekend there playing two bar shows of the kind we usually do: for a very small, but always enthusiastic audience. Sven: What are Kregel’s plans for the future? We hope to make music together for many more years, release EPs, and regularly be invited to play that music live. We like to let things happen naturally, without too much planning. Q: You do not hide the fact that the Post-Punk of the ’80s and ’90s has had a strong influence on your compositions. What exactly made those years and that musical style so magical, and what elements of it still remain today in Kregel’s sound? Bart: The three of us grew up in the 1980s, and that was when our musical tastes were formed. Although we did not know each other at the time, we were apparently all particularly drawn to (Post-)Punk and New-Wave, and to anything that leaned in that direction. It seems obvious to us that those influences resonate in the sound we produce in 2026, but we cannot pinpoint exactly which elements they are. Sven: In any case, it is not as though we had a very specific idea of the sound we wanted to pursue when Kregel was formed. We never even explicitly discussed it. The only starting points we had when we decided to continue as a trio were that the lyrics would be in Dutch, and that we would use a computer as our rhythm section. The ‘Kregel sound’ — insofar as such a thing can be said to exist, because our sound is evolving too — is therefore not the result of extensive prior discussion, but of playing together. The only criterion we use is that all three of us are happy with a song. Q: Internationally, choosing to sing in your native language, Dutch, can be seen as a challenge, but at the same time it highlights your originality—combined with lyrics that are sometimes humorous yet, in my opinion, still carry a certain depth. That raises the question: why singing in Dutch, what is this depths of the lyrical content and is it an option for you to ever sing in another language? Jeroen: As mentioned, choosing to write in Dutch was a conscious decision from the very beginning. We do not want to write throwaway songs, but at the same time, we do not want to put overly explicit ‘messages’ into our lyrics. We want to make songs about subjects and feelings that matter to us and occupy our minds, without wanting to impose anything on our audience. With Kregel, there is no finger-wagging; rather, we use down-to-earth and original ways of expressing our feelings about certain subjects, wrapped up in compact, almost slogan-like lyrics with a large dose of (dark) humour. Bart: All of that would not work for us in a language other than our mother tongue, even if this can be a barrier to our ‘international career’. Moreover, Dutch is a very evocative language, with lots of double meanings and idiomatic expressions, so it can occasionally make a perceptive listener raise an eyebrow. We briefly considered translating the lyrics when we were invited to England, but precisely because of those double meanings and idioms, we could not arrive at an acceptable result, so we decided against it. Sven: On the other hand, the ‘disadvantage’ of making music in a small language should not be overstated: we regularly play in the French-speaking part of Belgium, and the audience reactions are no different from those of Dutch-speaking audiences. We noticed the same thing in England when we were there: the unifying power of music should not be underestimated. Q: Another characteristic of Kregel is that, so far, you have only released EPs, each containing different, exclusive tracks. You are now at seven in total. Why this choice, and what is your stance on releasing a full-length album? Do albums still make sense in a world where most listeners rely on streaming platforms and curated playlists? Bart: The fact that we release our tracks in groups of four on EPs is actually purely coincidental, as is the case with many things involving Kregel. In 2016, we independently released a self-titled debut EP with four tracks, pressed onto 300 CDs. In 2019, we had 12 tracks ready that we wanted to release as an album, but once everything had been recorded in our home studio, the COVID crisis broke out… With the entire live sector shut down, we came up with a completely different strategy from quarantine: between June and September 2020, we released a new EP online on the 4th of every month. The first was the 2016 debut EP, which was remixed, remastered and released as “#1”. The next three were logically called “#2”, “#3” and “#4”. These were released online only, and each was accompanied by a video clip, in the hope of generating as much online attention as possible. Sven: We did not think the EP formula was such a bad idea, and when we had another eight  tracks ready in 2022, we released “#5” and “#6” online, one month apart. We did physically release both EPs on a vinyl album, with a “#5” side and a “#6” side. In the meantime, we have almost come to regard the idea of four-track EPs as self-evident, and so “#7” followed in March of this year. We are currently working on “#8”… Jeroen: It is not that we do not want to release an album, but our productivity is rather low, so it would take us two or three years to write and record enough material for one… For now, we are aiming for one EP a year (although we have to admit that even that is probably a little too ambitious for “#8”…), and that also keeps things a little exciting for us. Q: Speaking of those EPs, especially the latest “#7,” which took a while to arrive—by the way—to what extent is this new release different from, or innovative compared to, the previous ones? How did it come about? What were the different stages you went through, and what were the biggest challenges you had to overcome? Sven: The big difference between “#7” and its predecessors was that this latest EP was not recorded in our own home studio with Bart behind the controls. For this EP, we called on a good friend, Alessio Di Turi, who has a professional recording studio, and we spent three days there working on the recordings. By then, we knew what it was like to do everything ourselves, and we were particularly curious about the added value of a ‘real recording studio’, and we have to say that it pleasantly surprised us. Jeroen: Moreover, this way of working had the advantage of taking some of the pressure off Bart during the recording sessions, allowing him to concentrate fully on his musical contributions and leave the technical concerns to Alessio. Q: How does collaboration within Kregel work, and what creates the chemistry between you? By the way, what is your musical background? Bart: Our collaboration can be summed up briefly and concisely as ‘plug in and play’. We get together (almost) once a week at around 9 p.m. and play until about 11 p.m. After more than 15 years, we know each other inside out and know what to expect from one another. We create our songs together during these more or less weekly gatherings. Starting from a simple idea, we puzzle over the lyrics and music until that one magical moment when everything falls into place and we exchange a satisfied look of understanding: ‘OK, another song done!’ That process can go quickly, but sometimes it can be painfully slow: anywhere from a few rehearsals to ten or so. It has also happened that we spent five or six rehearsals tweaking a song before concluding at some point: ‘This isn’t going anywhere’… Without many words, we stop and move on to another idea… Different and better, no drama. Jeroen: We are not formally trained musicians and learned everything in the finest DIY Punk tradition. Bart has been the frontman of Vandal X and Flipo Mancini since his teens. I started a band when I was 16, in which I was the singer, but that role did not suit me. I stopped when I was 18 and bought a second-hand guitar. In the years that followed, I made a few half-hearted attempts to start new bands. It took many years before I happened to meet Sven and arranged to jam with him. That led to Feetfetish, and the rest is Kregel history. Sven: Before Feetfetish, I had never committed to a permanent band. I did have a guitar, which I learned to play without much of a plan, sometimes with friends, but it was only with Feetfetish that it became a regular thing. Jeroen: Those weekly rehearsals have by now become almost a physical necessity: putting the daily hassles aside and creating ‘Something Beautiful’ together with a few good friends — that is what it is all about for us! Sven: But there is also the romance of being ‘on the road’ together: the rituals of coffee breaks at motorway service stations, loading our gear, soundchecks, the concerts themselves, of course (and the kick they give!), packing everything up, and driving home at night… Bart: Not to forget the wonderful encounters! With organizers, promoters, venue volunteers, other bands, but above all with the audience, who are invariably enthusiastic. We seem to be part of a small but very welcoming scene of free-spirited people, connected by the magic of the underground. Q: You already mentioned it, but recently, you had the honor of opening for none other than P.I.L. here in Belgium. How was that experience, and what was the encounter like with the one and only Johnny ‘Rotten’ Lydon? Sven: Indeed, it was a great honor, even though we were filling in for the tour’s regular support act! We had been briefed beforehand that Mr. Lydon was rather ‘a man unto himself’ and did not like to be ‘bothered’ before or after a concert. Naturally, we respected that (the man had already been touring for months), and we were more than happy simply to be there at all and do our thing. Bart: Afterwards, we again received nothing but positive reactions to our gigs, along with excellent merch sales! Jeroen: Those two support slots were genuine milestones in Kregel’s existence! It was the first time we had played in such large, highly professional venues (Botanique in Brussels and TRIX in Antwerp), which were also almost sold out. What a luxury: perfect stage sound, and even a few stagehands at our disposal (as we discovered after we had already set up our gear…). All those circumstances, combined with the great reactions from the audience, made us feel as though we had risen above ourselves… Moreover, the very strong P.I.L. shows gave us, as ‘older youngsters’, hope for the future. Q: What else is written in the stars for Kregel? Sven: We have no idea. The only thing we do know is that we still get together every week with an enormous amount of pleasure, as we have been doing for more than 15 years, and that this has become an essential part of our existence. We hope that can continue for a long time, with the occasional concert (although we would like to play more shows than we actually do…), the release of new songs, and everything that comes with ‘being in a band together’, but above all the great pleasure we get from knowing that other people also enjoy what we do. Jeroen: After our two nights in the shadow of John Lydon, we agreed that we would at least keep going until we are 80… Bart: And now we can only hope that the stars won’t write a different story…

items.body: Fields of the Nephilim, the English gothic rock band from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, released “The Nephilim” on 5 September 1988 through Situation Two, an imprint of Beggars Banquet. The album turns 38 this year. It was the band’s second studio album, it followed “Dawnrazor” from 1987, and it entered the UK album chart at number 12. The record was made in a former courthouse. Sessions took place at The Justice Room in the Somerset countryside, a building where prisoners sentenced to death had been hanged on site. Bassist Tony Pettitt described the setting in a 2013 PopMatters retrospective on the album’s 25th year: “The place had a really cool vibe”. Mixing moved to Genetic Studios and the master was cut at Tape One. Sources differ on the production credit: the Situation Two sleeve lists Bill Buchanan as producer with the band credited in association, while Wikipedia gives the band itself. Brad Davis recorded the sessions, Timm Baldwin mixed, and Ian Gillespie handled pre-mastering. The line-up was Carl McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass, Peter Yates and Paul Wright on guitars, and Alexander “Nod” Wright on drums. ‘The Nephilim’ formats, tracklist and credits Situation Two issued the album in the UK as a gatefold LP with printed lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost”, and on CD and cassette. Rebel Rec. handled the German pressing through SPV, and Beggars Banquet released it in the United States with RCA. The vinyl runs eight tracks: “Endemoniada”, “The Watchman”, “Phobia”, “Moonchild”, “Chord of Souls”, “Celebrate”, “Love Under Will” and “Last Exit for the Lost”. The CD adds a ninth, “Shiva”, which had been the B-side of the “Moonchild” single. Chris Bigg designed the sleeve, Simon Larbalestier shot the outer photography, Julian Calverley the inner gatefold, and Lynn S supplied the lyric calligraphy. “Moonchild” reached number 28 in the UK singles chart, well above the number 75 the band had managed a year earlier with “Blue Water”. Several titles point outward: “Moonchild” shares its name with a novel by Aleister Crowley, “Love Under Will” takes a phrase from his Book of the Law, and the lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost” reference H. P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu. The opening track, “Endemoniada”, carries a sample of Ron Perlman growling “Penitenziagite!” as the hunchback Salvatore in the 1986 film “The Name of the Rose”. Beggars Archive returned to the album on 20 October 2023 with a double-LP reissue pressed on golden brown vinyl and expanded with three bonus tracks. About Fields of the Nephilim Carl McCoy, Tony Pettitt, Paul Wright, Alexander “Nod” Wright and saxophonist Gary Wisker formed Fields of the Nephilim in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, in 1984. The name refers both to the biblical race of angel-human hybrids and to the magnetic fields around the Earth. Peter Yates joined on guitar in 1985, the year the band put out its debut 12″ EP “Burning the Fields” on its own Tower Release label. Jungle Records picked the record up and put the band back in the studio for the “Returning to Gehenna” EP. Situation Two signed them in 1986 and issued the singles “Power” and “Preacher Man”. The first album, “Dawnrazor”, topped the UK indie chart in 1987, and “Blue Water” became their first entry on the UK singles chart. “The Nephilim” followed in 1988. “Psychonaut” arrived in May 1989 and peaked at number 35, its ten-minute running time pointing toward the more layered approach of “Elizium” in 1990. For that album the band moved up to the Beggars Banquet imprint and worked with Andy Jackson, an engineer for Pink Floyd and David Gilmour, in place of Bill Buchanan. Its lead single “For Her Light” clipped the UK top 40 in its first week, and a remixed “Sumerland (Dreamed)” reached number 37 that November. The band played its last shows of that era in 1991, a two-day Festival of Fire at the Town & Country Club in London, documented on the live album “Earth Inferno” and the video “Visionary Heads”. McCoy left the same year. The remaining members recruited singer Andy Delaney and continued as Rubicon, releasing “What Starts, Ends” in 1992 and “Room 101” in 1995. McCoy started Nefilim, whose album “Zoon” was held back by label disagreements until 1996. McCoy and Pettitt announced a return at a press conference during the Zillo Festival in Germany on 15 August 1998. The single “One More Nightmare (Trees Come Down)” came out on Jungle Records in May 2000, reworking two songs from “Burning the Fields”, and the band played Woodstage, Eurorock, Roskilde and M’era Luna that summer. Jungle issued “Fallen” in 2002 with licensees including Metropolis Records and SPV; the band disowned it, and only one of its songs has been played live. McCoy’s fourth full-length under the Fields of the Nephilim name, “Mourning Sun”, appeared in 2005 with a cover of Zager and Evans’ “In the Year 2525” as a bonus track on the first 5,000 copies. A new line-up played the London Astoria in May 2007, the first Fields of the Nephilim show in seven years, and headlined M’era Luna in 2008 in front of a crowd of more than 23,000. Recordings from two Shepherd’s Bush Empire nights became “Ceromonies (Ad Mortem Ad Vitam)”, released on McCoy’s Sacred Symphony label on 16 April 2012. Beggars Archive collected the first three studio albums, “Earth Inferno” and a singles-and-remixes disc in a five-album box in November 2013. McCoy said in July 2014 that the band was back in the studio; “Earthbound” and “Prophecy” were played live that December, and “Prophecy” was issued as a single on 17 March 2016, produced, engineered and mixed by McCoy and mastered by Maor Appelbaum. Guitarist Tom Edwards, who played with the band between 2008 and 2016, died of heart failure in January 2017 while touring the United States with Adam Ant, reported at the time in Fields of the Nephilim / Adam Ant guitarist Tom Edwards dies aged 41. Beggars Archive has kept the back catalogue moving since then, with the expanded “The Nephilim” in October 2023, a 30th anniversary red vinyl “Elizium” on 5 April 2024, and a remastered “Dawnrazor” on 12 December 2025. The current line-up is McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass and Gavin King and Adam Leach on guitars. Thirty-eight years on, “The Nephilim” still sits at the centre of that catalogue, between the indie-chart-topping “Dawnrazor” and the wider reach of “Elizium”.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — By now, It must be suitable for me to tip my cap to the Malcolm/Mark pairing, a London project that has kept a prolific and qualitative progression ( that confounded word, again!) and I have been following closely since I purchased the "Nostalgia for Infinity" (2020) album. Their recent output consists of three out and out jewels, which have been critically acclaimed, and there is no reason to doubt that this new 2026 effort would not make anyone lose their hair to baldness. With Parallel Lives, the dynamic duo throw no curves that may sidetrack their strengths, focusing on the premise that the shortest distance between two points may perhaps be a straight line, but why not offer 11 tracks (2 extras being radio edits), all neatly equivalent? "My Blistering Mind" could easily be referring to the blistering Gartland bass line that decorates this brainy track that seems to cause havoc with the splinters stuck in their collective cortex , both sides being roughed up with a punky tinge that has always been present in the HOGIA stylistic. Its not only a catchy opener but its obsessive quality is quantified by the backing vocal effort that really sets this track apart from the mundane. Coming as a wonderful surprise, "The Mandatory Prize" (rogue poetry in lotion!) keeps their quirky musical gift firmly tongue in cheek, a brooding critique of societal hypocrisy, which let's face it, is something only humans can indulge in with sadistic pleasure, save a hyena and perhaps also a scorpion (the first killing others for sheer pleasure and the other wilfully murdering themselves). Lose when you win, indeed. The musical tone is correctly pugnacious. Flip that damn switch and out of the wild blue yonder comes a gorgeous and charming instrumental that knocked me sideways, "Never Really Felt Like Home" conveys a sense of lukewarm regret, far from anger but surely in bed with despondence. Guest Kathryn Thomas uses a variety of flutes to underscore one of the finest melodies heard in recent years, a superb slice of yearning. Prog rapping comes unwrapped (clever again) on "Smile, Smile, Smile" , a shivering electronic riff skipping over an intense spoken word that starts out accepting and turning into gentlemanly rage. 'Nobody knows who you are', even yourself I guess and frankly, what is existence all about ? Accumulating wealth and power? No, the answer is in the title: be happy and smile, repeated three times for effect. Fertig !Jazz it up, will you now! "Intermission" has the Tangent/Andy Tillison vibe that highlights a wide range of classic mood swings (accent on the swing part) , a ruthless bass exercise (both musicians are incredible but I have a well-known fetish for the bass guitar and Gatland ranks as one of my perennial faves), a marvelous interlude that will set-up the suave beauty of the title track, a heart-felt love song that is progged up with delicate detail, and gratefully stripped down to the basics : voice, piano and distant percussion. And tons of fervent emotion, eyes closed, ears open. The chosen melodic line is another example of their attention to feeling ,a masterful stroke of genius. Waking up from the dream, prompted from a remote command , the somewhat more energetic "Eversion" revives the fiery anger this band manages on an even par with their melancholy, a slightly deranged and obsessive look into the mirror of past lives still unsettled. Essentially a vortex of circular sonic turbulence, the voice and that darn bass confusing the issues with a wide variety of counterstrokes and pushback. Malcolm finally whips out his electric guitar and goes on zippered tear, a short slash that only reinvigorates the urge to hold on and seek help. Seven minutes of intensity. Opting for an compulsive electronic diversion (which they use regularly but only with surgical precision) "Pretty Blue Fox" is another thrilling instrumental that certainly invokes images of parallel realms, a dreamscape of unusual consequence and open to individual conjecture. The keyboard work is exemplary (the piano in particular) and adapted to the overall tendency of this recording. Well played! Back to in-your-face simplicity on the ear-friendly "Just Another Thing", Malcolm speeding through the lyrics like an F1 McLaren race car, vroom-vroom pursuit, 'to add to the list', a checkered flag synthesizer flutter to keep the engines oiled, the bass pistons throttling loudly, and the rubber smoking. Punk-prog. Attached is the outro instrumental "Dropping the Mask", proving once and for evermore that the main attraction of this act is their aptitude to balance worded and non-worded material without losing any talent or identity . If the glove fits?The epic two-part finale "Just Hold On" is a glowing tribute to the hyperactive societal burden we must all bear, where time and space are blurred into an algo rhythmic smear that keeps us from restful peace of mind or quiet critical thinking. The opening choir section underlines that agony, the electric guitar somehow hopeful, the bass thoughtfully gentle, eventually building up the urgency that makes blood circulate in our veins, oxygenizing our brain as well as limbering up our machine's muscles. Malcolm vocal is more of a sermon to the times, the lyrics depressive and apathetic but the message combative and resilient. Its never too late. Happiness and contentment can be a as simple as a forceful decision, a basic choice, to just HOLD ON. Take my hand and get this album, it just might help the healing process we humans all deserve. Its not too late. The shortened radio edits of the first two tracks are oddly enough not edits as they are the same length or even longer than the originals, Brits have the best sense of humor, sardonic and off the wall. Their absolute finest effort by a country mile. Hats off !5 corresponding existences

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is an atmospheric quality to the guitar sound of Ian Alexander Griffiths, a guitarist born in Cologne, Germany, yet with one foot in America and the other in Europe, his musical interests shaped by his parents' dual heritage. He explores the English language, specifically how to communicate and convey feelings and ideas through it most effectively, using music as the vehicle. He is not alone in this endeavor; accompanied by keyboard, bass, and drums, the sound at times becomes cosmic, evoking a sci-fi epic. While there are echoes of Steven Wilson, his approach to the guitar draws comparisons to Steve Hackett, featuring a grand, expansive sound that isn't afraid to dip into hard rock influences or take a dark turn, as evidenced by the track "Exoplanet." The album is a cohesive whole, yet the first paradox, undoubtedly intentional, lies in the very concept of disconnection. Hints of a fusion style emerge in the guitar work, foreshadowing the solo career Alexander would eventually pursue.While more acoustic songs featuring impeccable technical execution, such as "Child of Our Times", may not stand out for their originality, it is in the more experimental instrumental tracks like "Five Bagger", where the guitar ventures into new territory, that Ter'Azur finds its strength. There are echoes of the Animals -era Pink Floyd, updated to transform that factory of analog smokestacks and floating pigs into a modern, digitized, and automated complex."Mass Hypnosis" is another highlight where the heavy guitar cuts through a wall of keyboards, breaking into a calm akin to blinding laser lights; the vocals are equally original, whispered, which makes them all the more menacing, while the quartet sounds incredibly tight. Once again, those solos that scale the crags, accompanied by the bass and carrying a touch of mystery in the notes, transport us to Spectral Mornings or Hackett's more recent material, until a heavy surge of keyboards dispels the mist."Beneath the Molten Sand," with its long, Arabic-inspired introduction, features a more settled vocal section that is better integrated musically. There are moments when the choir truly takes flight, with all four members singing, creating a genuinely oppressive atmosphere of tense anticipation that complements the composition."Nuke" stands out for the complexity of its arrangements within a layered rock sound, much like "Wayward Souls," which features a fusion style reminiscent of Pat Metheny during his own progressive phase. "Weather Report" is the album's title track and longest piece; while the vocal sections anchor it in a degree of predictability, the guitar work and instrumental rock passages elevate the song, offering surprises and introducing colors and textures that transcend a monochromatic blue.The album's title is highly revealing, referencing that transitional period when one drifts off, slipping into sleep while still awake. That transition shapes the album's trajectory, promising and accomplished, as it navigates the uncertain quest for a state beyond consciousness.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Madra Salach‘s “The Man Who Seeks Pleasure (Live from London)” was recorded on the last night of the band’s sold-out debut headline tour, at The Dome in Tufnell Park in March, and arrived on Island Records on 26 June. The song first appeared on the Dublin band’s debut EP, It’s a Hell of an Age, released in January, which reached number three on the Irish Albums Chart, broke into the UK’s Official Independent Albums Chart top ten and earned the band live sessions for BBC 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq and Radio 1’s New Music Fix. Paul Banks built the song around indulgence undercut by consequence, pleasure and pain framed as two names for the same want, setting the scene early with the image “lick the sugar off the cane.” The London version stretches that tension out with the full band: Jack Martin and Adam Cullen‘s guitar and mandolin lines wind around each other, Maxime Arnold‘s harmonium deepens the drone underneath, and Dara Duffy and Jack Lawlor push the song harder on drums and bass than the EP cut allows. Banks has said the recording comes from “the last show on our debut headline tour,” and that the band wanted a version built around the full arrangement rather than the more minimal EP take. The band follow the release with a run of summer festival dates including Electric Picnic and Green Man, before returning to headline UK and Irish venues in October. items.body: Review by tszirmay — Kansas. Toto, Len Dawson, Patrick Mahones and the band that put the Mid-West state on the prog billboards worldwide, wayward sons like dust in the wind. Here is Quivira , Jake Livgren on vocals (does the name ring a bell?), the thrilling Lisa Larue on keyboards, her recent Rematrination debut left me in awe. Filling out the trio is guitarist John Baker who has worked with Mars Hollow and Forever Twelve. Within a mere 6 seconds of the intro, "The Coming of the Spaniards", my experienced ears immediately sent the following message to my brain, 'this is going to be very very good'. Its all there: massive choirs echoing cross the sandy valleys, concentrated symphonics with a colossal Iberian influence on the acoustic guitar, interweaving conquering violins, elegance in the piano structure and loads of cinematic grandeur. Yes, I am still exhaling ?.On that note, "The Benefits of Breathing Quietly" has Joe Denizon's crafty violin leading the way, passing the baton to Jake's expansive voice, a commanding pulmonary delivery where both tone and delivery hold hands in interlocked splendour, and Lisa's synths flirt unashamedly with the catskin gasps. She also dazzles on the piano as well taking care of the programmed drums (which are expertly designed.A cunning play on words with "The Plain's Truth", equally clever musically, as the fluttering violin plays the lead to perfection, building up the fury courtesy of John's superlative note bending (both the 6 and 4 string varieties), a merging of sounds totally in harmony with one another, eventually painting the vast landscape of both arid mesas and endless grasslands beyond. The acoustic guitar cannot help to revive that Hispanic sentiment, a dramatic sonic statement of intent. Time to dive into more classic prog-rock initiatives, surely evoking the legendary Kansas overtly melodic bombast, Lisa Larue in particular shining brightly on her various keys, she is truly a star to reckon with. More passionate violin to remind us that its all about feeling, touch and caress. "Quivira Bound" becomes all fussed up with a twangy guitar solo that sparkles in the rain, the e-piano lull a momentary reflection of light, before Jake goes for another round on the microphone. Damn impressive. Wide screen smoothness on the ripping "Moving Forward", shifting gears into a musical cruise control, letting the electric guitar, violin and synths solo to their hearts content. Baker's raunchy axe will surely blow a few tumble weeds into the mix, a stunning spotlight that nails the tombstone coffin tight. The violin setting features a two-track splurge that is equally mind blowing. The programmed drums are stupendously effective here, some prog purists hate the idea as a rule but frankly, the technology has certainly evolved from the old TR-808, as the title may imply. This is a headline piece of musical genius. Everything changes on "The Turk/Follow the Wind", namely the mood, the sound and the vocal style, a shocking variation that gives more pavement to the highway ahead. The sultry violin commands the instrumental cavalry once again, leading the charge as the storytelling suggests a look back at times gone by, when nature held firm against the conquest of the wild, wild west . We now reach the heart of the sunrise, so to speak, with two of the longer tracks (both 7?8-minute range) that will define the core of the album, especially in a progressive context, as they are intricate workouts that ooze endeavour, aptitude and mature vision. "Nothing is Everything" is a fast-paced symphonic extravaganza that hesitates not one iota in getting into the nitty-gritty. Lisa's solo piano sections are to die for, the inserting violin sizzle adding to the fire, the arrangement expanding into a gargantuan crescendo that keeps accelerating into a near frenzy. Its so explosive and stimulating, and as the final segment reveals a gentler outcome, one realizes that the question has been answered. Nothing is everything. Spectacular. "Carved from the Sun" reveals a more groove orientation, almost like a driving down the freeway in a convertible, the throttling bass mercilessly crushing the gravel, the brassy guitar spiralling in full control, kicking up a vast wall of smoke that can be seen for miles and miles. The spirit is warm yet airy, bright and surely windy. This is 'close your eyes and imagine' style of prog that should impress even the most finnicky prog fans out there, equally grandiose and mesmerizing, and deeply committed to pleasure. I mean, wow!"Kicking Rocks" (a great way to damage your toes out in the mountains) expresses perfectly the foundation of this muscular piece, not at all 'hard or heavy' but certainly beefy and athletic. Lisa's piano proves her immense versatility, her fingers creating evocative images of strength and movement. When John decides that he needs to 'ramble on', he does so with gusto, bravado and tornado, flicking big swaths of thrills. Expertly planned album as this clearly is, the final two tracks seek to reestablish a connection with the opening tracks, the violin /piano interaction returning to the front of the stage on "Prelude to Anywhere /Weekend Conquistadors", a recurring vocal presentation where the epic story nears its natural conclusion. The upsurge is obvious, the mood settles and some brief narration expounds the message. I am 'Still Breathing", though barely, as the emotions I have felt listening to this work has overcome my sense of critical thinking, a somewhat similar effect as falling in love (where reason kneels before the heart), and the realization that this final and momentous piece encapsulates the entire hour and 6 minutes spent in its glorified presence. Surely, among the top candidates for album of the year but unchallengeable winner of debut of the year! The horse has run away?..5 Flight of eagles

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以1819年彼得卢屠杀为背景，通过原创歌曲重新讲述英国工人运动史上的关键事件。Sean Cooney联合Eliza Carthy、Sam Carter等音乐人，以小型合奏营造出从集会期待、屠杀恐慌到悲恸余波的完整情绪弧线。歌曲聚焦具体人物，如萨姆·班福德和玛丽·菲尔兹，并用三首短曲刻画士兵的傲慢与暴行。专辑以书籍形式附带当代信件与政治漫画，构成多媒体叙事。音乐本身为传统民谣框架下的声乐主导作品，旋律有力，歌词意象精炼，演唱富有情感。然而其风格局限于英国当代民谣，缺乏实验性或跨界融合元素，与偏好前卫、电子、爵士或世界音乐的口味匹配度较低。
